nodes.name: k-section problem
nodes.statement: Given a graph $G= (V,E)$, the $k$-section problem seeks to partition the vertices $V= V_1 \sqcup V_2 \sqcup \cdots \sqcup V_k$ into $k$ equal sets (or differing by at most 1) such that the number of edges between the distinct sets is minimized.
nodes.statement_short: Partition V into k equal parts minimizing the number of cross edges.

nodes.name: k-section width
nodes.statement: The minimum number of cross edges $w_k(G)$ thus obtained is referred to as the $k$-section width.

nodes.name: Max-Cut problem
nodes.statement: The related Max-Cut problem seeks to divide the vertices into two sets (not necessarily equal) such that the number of edges between the two sets is maximized.

nodes.name: Erdos-Renyi random graph
nodes.statement: An Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random graph $\mathrm{ER}_n(d/n)$ is constructed on $n$ vertices, where any two vertices share an edge with probability $d/n$, independently of each other.

nodes.name: d-regular random graph
nodes.statement: A $d$-regular random graph is drawn uniformly at random from the space of all $d$-regular graphs on $n$ vertices.

nodes.name: Bisection width phase transition for Erdos-Renyi graphs (Luczak-McDiarmid)
nodes.statement: For $d< 2\ln (2)$, the bisection width is exactly $0$ with high probability, while for $d > 2 \ln( 2)$, the bisection width is of order $n$, with high probability \cite{LM01}.
conclusions: the bisection width is exactly $0$ with high probability

nodes.name: Max-Cut phase transition for Erdos-Renyi graphs (Coppersmith et al.)
nodes.statement: The Max-Cut also undergoes a phase transition; for $d<1$, the difference between the total number of edges and the Max-Cut is of the constant order, while it is of the order $n$ for $d>1$~\cite{CGHS04}.
nodes.statement_short: For ER_n(d/n), edges minus Max-Cut is O(1) when d<1 and of order n when d>1.

nodes.name: Degree sequence
nodes.statement: Consider a degree sequence $\bld{d}=(d_1,d_2,\dots,d_n)$ on the vertex set $[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$.

nodes.name: Half-edges
nodes.statement: Equip vertex $j$ with $d_{j}$ stubs or \emph{half-edges}. Two half-edges create an edge once they are paired.

nodes.name: Total number of half-edges l_n
nodes.statement: Therefore, initially there are $\ell_n=\sum_{i \in [n]}d_i$ half-edges.

nodes.name: Configuration model
nodes.statement: Pick any one half-edge and pair it with a uniformly chosen half-edge from the remaining unpaired half-edges. Keep repeating the above procedure until all the unpaired half-edges are exhausted. The random graph constructed in this way is called the configuration model, and will henceforth be denoted by $\mathrm{CM}_{n}(\boldsymbol{d})$.
nodes.statement_short: Random multigraph obtained by uniformly pairing all half-edges.

nodes.name: Configuration model is simple with probability bounded away from zero
nodes.statement: Moreover, under rather general assumptions (see Assumption~\ref{assumption1} below), the asymptotic probability of the graph being simple is bounded away from zero~\cite{J09c}.
also_stated_at: It was shown in \cite{J09c} that under Assumption~\ref{assumption1}, the probability of the graph being simple is bounded away from zero.

nodes.name: Conditioned on simplicity the configuration model is uniform
nodes.statement: It can be shown that conditionally on $\mathrm{CM}_{n}(\boldsymbol{d})$ being simple, the law of such graphs is uniform over all possible simple graphs with degree sequence $\boldsymbol{d}$ (cf.~\cite[Proposition 7.7]{RGCN1}, \cite{JKLP93}).
nodes.origin_citation: van der Hofstad, RGCN Vol. 1, Prop. 7.7; Janson, Knuth, Luczak, Pittel 1993

nodes.name: Typical vertex
nodes.statement: A vertex chosen uniformly at random from the vertex set $[n]$, independently of the graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$ is called a \emph{typical} vertex.

nodes.name: Degree of a typical vertex D_n
nodes.statement: Let $D_n$ be the degree of a typical vertex.

nodes.name: Assumption 1 (degree sequence regularity)
nodes.statement: \normalfont Let $\bld{d} = \bld{d}_n$ be a degree sequence on $[n]$. The sequence of degree sequences $(\bld{d}_n)_{n\geq 1}$ is such that \begin{enumerate}[a.] \item $D_n\ensuremath{\xrightarrow{d}} D$ (\emph{weak convergence of the degree of a typical vertex}); \item $\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D_n]\to \ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D]$, and $\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D_n^2]\to\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D^2]$ (\emph{moment assumptions}); \item $\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}(D=1)>0$ (\emph{positive proportion of degree one vertices}). \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: D_n converges weakly to D with converging first two moments, and P(D=1)>0.
nodes.label: assumption1

nodes.name: Criticality parameter nu
nodes.statement: The phase transition occurs when the value of the parameter \begin{equation} \nu : = \frac{\expt{D(D-1)}}{\expt{D}} \end{equation} exceeds one (cf.~\cite{JL09}).

nodes.name: Criticality parameter nu
nodes.statement: \nu : = \frac{\expt{D(D-1)}}{\expt{D}}
nodes.label: eq:nu

nodes.name: Generating function g_D and root xi
nodes.statement: More precisely, let $g_D(x):=\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[x^D]$ be the probability generating function of $D$, and let $\xi$ be the unique nonzero solution to the equation $g_D'(x)=\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D] x$.

nodes.name: Asymptotic giant proportion eta
nodes.statement: Define \begin{equation} \eta=1-g_D(\xi). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Giant component proportion eta
nodes.statement: \eta=1-g_D(\xi).
nodes.label: defn:eta

nodes.name: i-th largest component
nodes.statement: For $i\geq 1$, denote the $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ largest component of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$ by $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (i)}$.

nodes.name: Giant component of the configuration model (Janson-Luczak)
nodes.statement: Consider \ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}\ satisfying {\rm Assumption~\ref{assumption1}}. Then, \begin{enumerate}[{\normalfont (i)}] \item $|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}|/n\ensuremath{\xrightarrow{\mathbbm{P}}} \eta$, as $n\to\infty$, where $\eta$ is as defined in \eqref{defn:eta}. Further, $\eta >0$ if and only if $\nu>1.$ \item Moreover, $|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (i)}|/n\ensuremath{\xrightarrow{\mathbbm{P}}} 0$, as $n\to\infty$, for all $i\geq 2$. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: $|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}|/n\ensuremath{\xrightarrow{\mathbbm{P}}} \eta$, as $n\to\infty$
$\eta >0$ if and only if $\nu>1.$

nodes.name: Notation for k-section width and Max-Cut
nodes.statement: For any graph $G$, the $k$-section width and Max-Cut are denoted by $w_k(G)$ and ${\sf{MaxCut}}(G)$, respectively.

nodes.name: Mean degree mu
nodes.statement: We denote $$ \mu=\expt{D} $$ to be the (asymptotic) expected degree of a typical vertex.

nodes.name: Vertex degree d_v and counts n_k
nodes.statement: The degree of a vertex $v$ is denoted by $d_v$, and the number of vertices of degree $k$ by $n_k$, $k\geq 0$.

nodes.name: Adjacency notation
nodes.statement: If two vertices $u$ and $v$ share an edge, then we write $u\leftrightsquigarrow v$.

nodes.name: Neighborhood N[U,1] and r-neighborhood N[U,r]
nodes.statement: For a nonempty subset $U\subseteq [n]$ of vertices, the neighborhood (or 1-neighborhood) is defined as $$\mathcal{N}[U,1]:= U\cup \{v\in[n]:u\leftrightsquigarrow v\mbox{ for some }u\in U\},$$ and the $r$-neighborhood is defined as $\mathcal{N}[U,r]:=\mathcal{N}[\mathcal{N}[U,r-1],1]$, $r>1$.

nodes.name: Half-edge set S(A) and edge count E(A,A^c)
nodes.statement: For any subset of vertices $A$, we denote the half-edges incident to the vertices in $A$ by $S(A)$, and the number of edges between $A$ and $A^c$ by $E(A,A^c)$.

nodes.name: Double factorial
nodes.statement: For any integer $m\geq 1$, we denote $(2m)!! := (2m-1)(2m-3)\cdots 1$.

nodes.name: With high probability
nodes.statement: For a sequence of probability measures $(\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}_n)_{n\geq 1}$, the sequence of events $(\mathcal{E}_n)_{n\geq 1}$ is said to hold \emph{with high probability} if $\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}_n(\mathcal{E}_n)\to 1$.

nodes.name: Little o in probability
nodes.statement: For two sequences of random variables $(X_n)_{n\geq 1}$, and $(Y_n)_{n\geq 1}$, we write $X_n = \ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(Y_n)$ to denote that $X_n/Y_n\xrightarrow{\scriptscriptstyle \ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}} 0$.

nodes.name: Phase transition of the k-section width
nodes.statement: Consider $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$ satisfying {\rm Assumption~\ref{assumption1}}, and let $k\geq 2$ be an integer. Then $w_k(\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})})$ exhibits a phase transition around $\eta =1/k$. More precisely, \begin{enumerate}[{\normalfont (i)}] \item If $\eta <1/k$, then with high probability $w_k(\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})})\leq k/2$; \item If $\eta >1/k$, then there exists $\zeta>0$, such that with high probability $w_k(\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})})>\zeta n$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof outline of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement: Roughly speaking, when $\eta<1/k$, the strategy is to distribute all the components of size at least 3 among $k$ partitions as evenly as possible, and then to add the components of size at most 2 to balance the partitions. Since the size of the largest component is smaller than $n/k$ and the other components are very small ($o(n)$) in size, a $k$-partition can be made using the components of size at least 3, with at most $n/k$ vertices in each part. Because there are sufficiently many components of size at most~2 (Lemma~\ref{lem:num-pairs}), these can be used to balance the partitions. The latter step results in at most $k/2$ cross edges between the partitions. The above proof outline for the subcritical case is formalized in Section~\ref{ssec:ksection-subcrit}. Alternatively, when $\eta>1/k$, the size of the largest connected component is more than $n/k$. Therefore, in order to split the graph into $k$ equal partitions, the largest component must be split into at least two (possibly unequal) parts, each containing a positive proportion of vertices, and from the structural properties of the largest component, we show that with high probability this creates $\Theta(n)$ cross edges.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: subcritically pack components greedily and balance with size-2 components; supercritically the giant must be split, costing Theta(n) edges.

nodes.statement: Roughly speaking, when $\eta<1/k$, the strategy is to distribute all the components of size at least 3 among $k$ partitions as evenly as possible, and then to add the components of size at most 2 to balance the partitions.
nodes.statement_short: Distribute large components evenly, then balance with components of size at most 2.

nodes.name: Balance with small components
nodes.statement: Because there are sufficiently many components of size at most~2 (Lemma~\ref{lem:num-pairs}), these can be used to balance the partitions. The latter step results in at most $k/2$ cross edges between the partitions. The above proof outline for the subcritical case is formalized in Section~\ref{ssec:ksection-subcrit}.
nodes.statement_short: Many size-2 components balance the parts at a cost of at most k/2 cross edges.

nodes.name: Supercritical case
nodes.statement: Alternatively, when $\eta>1/k$, the size of the largest connected component is more than $n/k$. Therefore, in order to split the graph into $k$ equal partitions, the largest component must be split into at least two (possibly unequal) parts, each containing a positive proportion of vertices, and from the structural properties of the largest component, we show that with high probability this creates $\Theta(n)$ cross edges.
nodes.statement_short: The giant must be split, creating Theta(n) cross edges.

nodes.name: Optimality of the subcritical k-section bound
nodes.statement: \normalfont \cite[Theorem 1]{LM01} establishes that the $k$-section width is exactly zero below a critical threshold given by $\eta = 1/k$. This holds for the Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi case due to the natural presence of many isolated vertices. For a general configuration model, this is not necessarily true, and therefore, Theorem \ref{thm:min-bis}~(i) is indeed the best possible result that one can hope for in this case. In particular, if we assume the presence of a positive fraction of isolated vertices in the degree sequence, then using Lemma~\ref{lem:graph-sub} below, we recover the same result as in~\cite{LM01}.
nodes.statement_short: Without isolated vertices the bound k/2 is best possible; with a positive fraction of isolated vertices the width is zero, as for Erdos-Renyi graphs.
nodes.label: rem:isolated-vert

nodes.name: Distance from bipartiteness DistBip(G)
nodes.statement: The difference between the total number of edges and the Max-Cut is often referred to as the \emph{distance from bipartiteness} of a graph $G$, and will be denoted by ${\sf DistBip}(G)$. In other words, ${\sf DistBip}(G)$ counts the minimum number of edges in $G$ to be deleted in order to make it bipartite.

nodes.name: Heuristic for the Max-Cut phase transition
nodes.statement: The heuristic behind this phase transition is that when $\nu<1$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$ is \emph{roughly} a collection of trees and a \emph{finite} number of unicyclic components. The trees do not contribute any edge to ${\sf DistBip}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})})$ at all, and the unicyclic components with an odd cycle (i.e., containing an odd number of edges) contributes at most one to the ${\sf DistBip}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})})$. On the other hand, when $\nu>1$, this is no longer true, and any partition must leave $\Theta(n)$ edges uncut.
nodes.statement_short: Heuristic: subcritical graph is trees plus finitely many unicyclic components, each odd cycle costing one edge; supercritically Theta(n) edges stay uncut.

nodes.name: Results transfer to simple and inhomogeneous random graphs
nodes.statement: \normalfont It was shown in \cite{J09c} that under Assumption~\ref{assumption1}, the probability of the graph being simple is bounded away from zero. Thus the phase transition results in Theorems~\ref{thm:min-bis}~and~\ref{thm:max-cut} also hold for the uniformly chosen simple graph with a prescribed degree sequence. Hence, all the results proved in the paper are true also for $\ensuremath{\mathrm{ER}_n(d/n)}$, as well as the generalized random graphs under appropriate conditions \cite[Theorem 6.15]{RGCN1} on the weight sequence $\boldsymbol{w}$. In fact, the results are true for an even more general class of inhomogeneous random graph models (cf. \cite[Theorem 6.18]{RGCN1}).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: Suppose that $G$ contains $m_{ 2}$ components of size more than 2, and enumerate them as $C_1$, $C_2$, $\ldots, C_{m_{2}}$ with sizes $c_1\geq \dots\geq c_{m_2},$ respectively (ties can be broken arbitrarily). We construct $k$ partitions $V_1, V_2,\ldots, V_k$ sequentially as follows. Define $V_1(1)=C_1$, and $V_i(1)=\emptyset$ for $i=1,\ldots,k$. For $2\leq t\leq m_2$, $$V_i(t) = \begin{cases} V_i(t-1)\cup C_t\quad\text{if}\quad i = \min\{j:|V_j(t-1)\cup C_t|\leq n/k\},\\ V_i(t-1)\quad\qquad\text{otherwise}, \end{cases}$$ i.e., sequentially at each step add all the vertices in components of size more than 2, to the partitions in a way such that the size of each partition does not exceed $n/k$. The claim below establishes that the above steps are feasible. \begin{claim} For all $2\leq t\leq m_2$, $\min\{j:|V_j(t-1)\cup C_t|\leq n/k\}\leq k$. \end{claim} \begin{claimproof} Note that, due to condition~(i), $|V_i(1)|\leq n/k$. Now, if possible assume that at step $t_0\leq m_2$, $|V_j(t_0-1)\cup C_{t_0}|= |V_j(t_0-1)|+| C_{t_0}|>n/k$ for all $j=1,\ldots,k$. Summing over $j$, we have \begin{align*} \sum_{j=1}^k|V_j(t_0-1)|+k| C_{t_0}|>n \implies | C_{t_0}|>\frac{n}{k}-\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^k|V_j(t_0-1)|\geq \frac{n}{k} - \frac{n-rn}{k}, \end{align*} due to condition (ii). This in turn implies $|C_{t_0}|>\frac{rn}{k},$ which contradicts condition~(iii). \end{claimproof} After step $t=m_2$, we first add the components of size~2 and finally components of size~1 (the isolated vertices), if any. Observe that components of size~1,~2 can be added to the partitions such that each partition is of size $\lfloor n/k\rfloor$ or $\lfloor n/k\rfloor+1$, there are no cross edges between the partitions, and the number of vertices remaining to be included in any partition is at most $k-1$. Now, if $\#\{i:c_i = 1\} \geq k-1$, then at the last step the remaining vertices must be isolated ones, and these do not create any cross edge, and thus the $k$-section width is exactly zero. Otherwise, the remaining $k-1$ vertices can form at most $k/2$ cross edges (the worst case being there are no isolated vertices).

nodes.statement: It is worthwhile to note that the 2-core of any connected graph is also connected.

nodes.name: k-core peeling algorithm
nodes.statement: Algorithmically, the $k$-core of a graph can be obtained by sequentially deleting the vertices of degree less than $k$ along with all their incident edges, until all the vertices in the remaining graph have degree more than $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeatedly delete vertices of degree below k with their edges until none remain.

nodes.name: Delete low-degree vertices
nodes.statement: sequentially deleting the vertices of degree less than $k$ along with all their incident edges
nodes.statement_short: Remove a vertex of degree less than k and its edges.

nodes.name: Stopping rule
nodes.statement: until all the vertices in the remaining graph have degree more than $k$
nodes.statement_short: Stop when every remaining vertex has large degree.

nodes.name: Nested cores and forest outside the 2-core
nodes.statement: Observe that, $V^{k}\supseteq V^{k+1}$, and the subgraph induced by $V\setminus V^{2}$ is a forest.

nodes.name: 2-core of the giant component
nodes.statement: As explained above, the largest connected component $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$ can be decomposed into two disjoint subsets of vertices: the 2-core $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2$, and a forest of vertex-disjoint trees hanging from the 2-core.

nodes.name: Proof outline of Proposition 4.3
nodes.statement: Informally speaking, the 2-core is the denser part of the graph. Therefore, at a high level, splitting the 2-core into two parts, each containing a positive proportion of vertices, is in general \emph{costly}, and would lead to formation of a \emph{huge} number of cross edges. Thus the optimal strategy might be to \emph{peel off} the hanging trees, since moving each hanging tree to some other partition would form precisely one cross-edge. But in that case also, we show that the number of vertices in each of the hanging trees are small (essentially finite), and hence in order to move $\Theta(n)$ vertices to some other partition, $\Theta(n)$ trees must be cut, and thus, $\Theta(n)$ cross edges must be created. To formalize the above heuristics, the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop-no-e-d-cut} breaks into two key steps, each being true with high probability: \begin{enumerate}[{\normalfont (i)}] \item The hanging trees are not heavy, in the sense that peeling off a small number of them cannot separate out a large number of vertices. This is formalized in Lemma~\ref{lem:thin-tree}. \item The 2-core does not have an $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-cut, which is stated in Lemma~\ref{lem-epsilon-delta-2-core}. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: splitting the dense 2-core is costly, and hanging trees are thin, so moving Theta(n) vertices cuts Theta(n) trees.

nodes.name: 2-core is costly to split
nodes.statement: Informally speaking, the 2-core is the denser part of the graph. Therefore, at a high level, splitting the 2-core into two parts, each containing a positive proportion of vertices, is in general \emph{costly}, and would lead to formation of a \emph{huge} number of cross edges.
nodes.statement_short: Splitting the dense 2-core creates many cross edges.

nodes.name: Hanging trees are thin
nodes.statement: Thus the optimal strategy might be to \emph{peel off} the hanging trees, since moving each hanging tree to some other partition would form precisely one cross-edge. But in that case also, we show that the number of vertices in each of the hanging trees are small (essentially finite), and hence in order to move $\Theta(n)$ vertices to some other partition, $\Theta(n)$ trees must be cut, and thus, $\Theta(n)$ cross edges must be created.
nodes.statement_short: Peeling hanging trees costs one edge each, but trees are small, so Theta(n) edges are still needed.

nodes.name: Two key steps
nodes.statement: To formalize the above heuristics, the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop-no-e-d-cut} breaks into two key steps, each being true with high probability:
nodes.statement_short: The proof splits into two lemmas.

nodes.name: (i) Thin trees
nodes.statement: The hanging trees are not heavy, in the sense that peeling off a small number of them cannot separate out a large number of vertices. This is formalized in Lemma~\ref{lem:thin-tree}.
nodes.statement_short: Hanging trees are not heavy (Lemma 4.4).

nodes.name: (ii) Well-connected core
nodes.statement: The 2-core does not have an $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-cut, which is stated in Lemma~\ref{lem-epsilon-delta-2-core}. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The 2-core has no (epsilon,delta)-cut (Lemma 4.5).

nodes.name: Hanging trees T_h
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathcal{T}_h$, the set of all trees attached with the 2-core of $\mathscr{C}_{(1)}$, i.e., $T\in \mathcal{T}_h$ if and only if the subgraph in $\mathscr{C}_{(1)}$ induced by $T$ is a tree, $T\cap \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2 =\emptyset $, and there exists only one vertex $v_T\in \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2$ that shares an edge with some vertex in $T$.

nodes.name: Root w_T of a hanging tree
nodes.statement: We always assume that each tree $T \in \mathcal{T}_h$ is rooted at the unique point $w_T$ such that $(v_T,w_T)$ is an edge and $v_T\in\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2$.

nodes.name: Hanging trees are not heavy
nodes.statement: For any $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta=\delta_1(\varepsilon)>0$, such that with high probability, any collection $\mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_h$ of $\delta n$ trees contain at most $\varepsilon n$ vertices in total.
conclusions: there exists $\delta=\delta_1(\varepsilon)>0$, such that with high probability, any collection $\mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_h$ of $\delta n$ trees contain at most $\varepsilon n$ vertices in total
nodes.label: lem:thin-tree

nodes.name: No (epsilon,delta)-cut in the 2-core
nodes.statement: For any $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta = \delta_2(\varepsilon) > 0$ such that with high probability, $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2 $ does not have any $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-cut.
conclusions: there exists $\delta = \delta_2(\varepsilon) > 0$ such that with high probability, $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2 $ does not have any $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-cut
nodes.label: lem-epsilon-delta-2-core

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.3
nodes.statement: Fix any $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $\delta = \min\{\delta_1(\varepsilon/2), \delta_2(\varepsilon/2)\}$, where $\delta_1(\varepsilon)$ and $\delta_2(\varepsilon)$ are as in Lemmas~\ref{lem:thin-tree} and~\ref{lem-epsilon-delta-2-core}, respectively. We now claim that for this choice of $\delta$, there is no $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-cut in $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}$. Indeed, existence of an $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-cut in $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}$ implies that there exists $\delta n$ edges, whose removal splits $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}$ into two parts, both containing at least $\varepsilon n$ vertices. Observe that due to the choice of $\delta$, removal of any set of $\delta n$ edges can separate out at most $\varepsilon n/2$ vertices belonging to $\cup_{T\in\mathcal{T}_h}\{T\}$, and at most $\varepsilon n/2$ vertices belonging to $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2 $ with high probability, and the proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Choose delta from Lemmas 4.4 and 4.5 at epsilon/2: delta n edge removals separate at most epsilon n/2 tree vertices and epsilon n/2 core vertices.

nodes.name: Choose delta
nodes.statement: Fix any $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $\delta = \min\{\delta_1(\varepsilon/2), \delta_2(\varepsilon/2)\}$, where $\delta_1(\varepsilon)$ and $\delta_2(\varepsilon)$ are as in Lemmas~\ref{lem:thin-tree} and~\ref{lem-epsilon-delta-2-core}, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Set delta as the minimum of the constants from Lemmas 4.4 and 4.5 at epsilon/2.

nodes.name: Claim: no cut for this delta
nodes.statement: We now claim that for this choice of $\delta$, there is no $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-cut in $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}$. Indeed, existence of an $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-cut in $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}$ implies that there exists $\delta n$ edges, whose removal splits $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}$ into two parts, both containing at least $\varepsilon n$ vertices. Observe that due to the choice of $\delta$, removal of any set of $\delta n$ edges can separate out at most $\varepsilon n/2$ vertices belonging to $\cup_{T\in\mathcal{T}_h}\{T\}$, and at most $\varepsilon n/2$ vertices belonging to $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2 $ with high probability, and the proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Show no (epsilon,delta)-cut exists in the giant for this delta.

nodes.name: Cut means few edges separate many vertices
nodes.statement: Indeed, existence of an $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-cut in $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}$ implies that there exists $\delta n$ edges, whose removal splits $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}$ into two parts, both containing at least $\varepsilon n$ vertices.
nodes.statement_short: A cut means delta n edges split the giant into two parts of epsilon n vertices.

nodes.name: Apply both lemmas
nodes.statement: Observe that due to the choice of $\delta$, removal of any set of $\delta n$ edges can separate out at most $\varepsilon n/2$ vertices belonging to $\cup_{T\in\mathcal{T}_h}\{T\}$, and at most $\varepsilon n/2$ vertices belonging to $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2 $ with high probability, and the proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: By the lemmas, delta n edges separate at most epsilon n/2 tree and epsilon n/2 core vertices.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.4
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemma 4.6 (small sets have small r-neighborhood degree sums) and Lemma 4.7 (few vertices lie deep in hanging trees).

nodes.name: First ingredient: Lemma 4.6
nodes.statement: The proof consists of two main steps. The first step establishes a property of the underlying degree sequence, which states that the sum of the degrees of `small' number of vertices is `small'. \begin{lemma} Under Assumption~\ref{assumption1}.\ref{assumption1-2}, given any $\varepsilon, r >0$, there exists $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon, r) >0$, such that for all sufficiently large $n$, the sum of degrees of the $r$-neighborhood of \emph{any} $\delta n$ vertices is at most~$\varepsilon n$, i.e. $\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}[U,r]}d_i<\varepsilon n$ uniformly over all subsets $U\subseteq [n]$ such that $|U|< \delta n$. \end{lemma}
nodes.statement_short: State Lemma 4.6 on degree sums of r-neighborhoods of small sets.

nodes.name: Small sets have small neighborhood degree sums
nodes.statement: Under Assumption~\ref{assumption1}.\ref{assumption1-2}, given any $\varepsilon, r >0$, there exists $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon, r) >0$, such that for all sufficiently large $n$, the sum of degrees of the $r$-neighborhood of \emph{any} $\delta n$ vertices is at most~$\varepsilon n$, i.e. $\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}[U,r]}d_i<\varepsilon n$ uniformly over all subsets $U\subseteq [n]$ such that $|U|< \delta n$.
conclusions: there exists $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon, r) >0$, such that for all sufficiently large $n$, the sum of degrees of the $r$-neighborhood of \emph{any} $\delta n$ vertices is at most~$\varepsilon n$
nodes.label: lem:small-nbd

nodes.name: Second ingredient: Lemma 4.7
nodes.statement: In the second step we show that $r$ can be chosen large enough, so that with high probability, the total number of vertices at depth more than $r$ in all hanging trees combined, is arbitrarily `small'. This is formalized in Lemma~\ref{lem:small-hanging-trees}. \begin{lemma} For any $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $r=r(\varepsilon)>0$ such that with high probability $$\left|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}\setminus\mathcal{N}[\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2,r]\right|<\varepsilon n.$$ \end{lemma}
nodes.statement_short: State Lemma 4.7 on vertices deep in hanging trees.

nodes.name: Few vertices far from the 2-core
nodes.statement: For any $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $r=r(\varepsilon)>0$ such that with high probability $$\left|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}\setminus\mathcal{N}[\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2,r]\right|<\varepsilon n.$$
conclusions: there exists $r=r(\varepsilon)>0$ such that with high probability $$\left|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}\setminus\mathcal{N}[\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2,r]\right|<\varepsilon n.$$
nodes.statement_short: For large r, whp fewer than epsilon n giant vertices are outside the r-neighborhood of the 2-core.
nodes.label: lem:small-hanging-trees

nodes.name: Equivalent restatement
nodes.statement: Given Lemmas~\ref{lem:small-nbd} and~\ref{lem:small-hanging-trees}, the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:thin-tree} can now be completed. Consider the following equivalent re-statement of Lemma~\ref{lem:thin-tree}: \begin{quotation} \noindent For any $\varepsilon, \beta>0$, there exists $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon)>0$ and $n_0= n_0(\varepsilon, \beta)$, for which, the probability that there exists a subset $\mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_h$ with $|\mathcal{T}|<\delta n$ and $|\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal{T}}\{T\}|\geq \varepsilon n$, is at most $\beta$ for all $n\geq n_0$. \end{quotation}
nodes.statement_short: Restate Lemma 4.4 with explicit probability beta and threshold n_0.

nodes.name: Choose r via Lemma 4.7
nodes.statement: To show the above statement, fix any $\varepsilon, \beta>0$. Using Lemma~\ref{lem:small-hanging-trees}, choose $r=r(\varepsilon/2)$ and $n_1 = n_1(\varepsilon/2,\beta)$, such that for all $n\geq n_1$, $$\prob{\left|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}\setminus\mathcal{N}[\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2,r]\right|\geq\frac{\varepsilon n}{2}}<\beta.$$
nodes.statement_short: Pick r so that few vertices lie beyond depth r from the 2-core.

nodes.name: Choose delta via Lemma 4.6
nodes.statement: Also, appealing to Lemma~\ref{lem:small-nbd}, we choose $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon/2, r)$ and $n_2 = n_2(\varepsilon,r)$, such that for all $n\geq n_2$, $\nexists\ U\subseteq V$ with $|U|< \delta n$ and $\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}[U,r]}d_i\geq \varepsilon n/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick delta so r-neighborhoods of fewer than delta n vertices have small degree sum.

nodes.name: Split heavy collection
nodes.statement: Now observe that if there exists a subset $\mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_h$ with $|\mathcal{T}|<\delta n$ and $|\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal{T}}\{T\}|\geq \varepsilon n$, then $$\text{either}\quad\bigg|\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{N}[w_T,r]\bigg|>\frac{\varepsilon n}{2} \quad \text{or}\quad \bigg|\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal{T}}\{T\}\setminus \bigcup_{T\in\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{N}[w_T,r]\bigg|>\frac{\varepsilon n}{2},$$ where $w_T$ is the unique vertex in $T$ that has a neighboring vertex in $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2$.
nodes.statement_short: A heavy collection of few trees has many vertices near the roots or far from them.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Choose $n_0 = \max\{n_1,n_2\}$ so that, for all $n\geq n_0$, the probability of the first event is 0, and that of the latter event is at most $\beta$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: For n >= n_0 the first event is impossible and the second has probability at most beta.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.6
nodes.statement: Fix any $\varepsilon>0$. We first verify the case when $r=1$ and prove this lemma by induction. Due to Assumption \ref{assumption1}\ref{assumption1-2}, $K=K(\varepsilon)>0$ can be chosen such that for all sufficiently large $n$, \begin{equation} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in [n]}d_i\ind{d_i>K} < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}. \end{equation} Take $\delta = \varepsilon/ (2K)$, and fix any $V\subseteq [n]$ with $|V|< \delta n$. Then, \begin{equation} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in V}d_i \leq \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i\in V}d_i\ind{d_i\leq K}+ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in [n]}d_i\ind{d_i>K} < \varepsilon. \end{equation} Now suppose that Lemma~\ref{lem:small-nbd} holds for some $r>0$. Choose $\delta_1=\delta(\varepsilon,1)$, and $\delta = \delta(\delta_1,r)$. Notice that for any $U\subseteq [n]$ with $|U|<\delta n$, $|\mathcal{N}[U,r]|<\delta_1 n$, and thus, $\sum_{i\in \mathcal{N}[U,r+1]}d_i=\sum_{i\in \mathcal{N}[\mathcal{N}[U,r],1]}d_i <\varepsilon n $.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on r: the base case truncates degrees at K using uniform integrability; the step applies the r=1 case to the r-neighborhood.

nodes.name: Induction plan
nodes.statement: Fix any $\varepsilon>0$. We first verify the case when $r=1$ and prove this lemma by induction.
nodes.statement_short: Prove the r=1 case, then induct on r.

nodes.name: Base case r=1
nodes.statement: Due to Assumption \ref{assumption1}\ref{assumption1-2}, $K=K(\varepsilon)>0$ can be chosen such that for all sufficiently large $n$, \begin{equation} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in [n]}d_i\ind{d_i>K} < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}. \end{equation} Take $\delta = \varepsilon/ (2K)$, and fix any $V\subseteq [n]$ with $|V|< \delta n$. Then, \begin{equation} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in V}d_i \leq \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i\in V}d_i\ind{d_i\leq K}+ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in [n]}d_i\ind{d_i>K} < \varepsilon. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Truncate degrees at K and take delta=epsilon/(2K).

nodes.name: Truncated degree sum
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in [n]}d_i\ind{d_i>K} < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}.

nodes.name: Degree sum of small sets
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in V}d_i \leq \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i\in V}d_i\ind{d_i\leq K}+ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in [n]}d_i\ind{d_i>K} < \varepsilon.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Now suppose that Lemma~\ref{lem:small-nbd} holds for some $r>0$. Choose $\delta_1=\delta(\varepsilon,1)$, and $\delta = \delta(\delta_1,r)$. Notice that for any $U\subseteq [n]$ with $|U|<\delta n$, $|\mathcal{N}[U,r]|<\delta_1 n$, and thus, $\sum_{i\in \mathcal{N}[U,r+1]}d_i=\sum_{i\in \mathcal{N}[\mathcal{N}[U,r],1]}d_i <\varepsilon n $.
nodes.statement_short: The r-neighborhood of a small set is small, so the base case applies to it.

nodes.name: Road-map for the proof of Lemma 4.7
nodes.statement: Observe that for any fixed $r>0$, and given any random observation $G$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$, $\left|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}\setminus\mathcal{N}[\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2,r]\right| = n\prob{V_n\in \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}\setminus\mathcal{N}[\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2,r]\given \ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}=G}$, where we recall that $V_n$ denotes a typical vertex. Therefore, it is enough to show that for any $\varepsilon>0$, $r= r(\varepsilon)$ can be chosen large enough, such that $$\prob{V_n\in \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}\setminus\mathcal{N}[\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2,r]\given \ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}= G}\ensuremath{\xrightarrow{\mathbbm{P}}} \varepsilon'<\varepsilon, \quad \text{as}\quad n\to\infty.$$ However, it is challenging to obtain the latter probability. For this reason, we will use the local event approximation technique, a key element in the study of sparse random graphs \cite{RGCN1,RGCN2,JLR00,BJM07,J08,BJR07}. In particular, our results for the configuration model mirror the ones proved in~\cite{BJR07} in the context of inhomogeneous random graphs. Roughly speaking, the crucial idea is based upon two observations: \begin{enumerate}[{\normalfont (i)}] \item The local neighborhood of a typical vertex resembles a branching process, i.e., with high probability, the breadth-first-search (BFS) exploration starting from $V_n$ up to suitable depth can be coupled with a branching process. This is formally stated in Proposition~\ref{prop-coupling}. \item Looking at the local neighborhood of $V_n$ up to suitable distance, it can be determined whether $V_n$ is near the 2-core. More specifically, the event that $V_n$ is within the $r$ neighborhood of the 2-core, is asymptotically `equivalent' to the event that for some $L_n \to \infty$, there exists two vertex disjoint paths of length $L_n$ from a vertex within the $r$ neighborhood of $V_n$. This fact is later formalized in Lemma~\ref{lem:loc-event-approx}. \end{enumerate} The proof follows once we have these ingredients in place.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the probability that a typical vertex is near the 2-core, approximated by a local branching-process event.

nodes.name: Reduce to a typical vertex
nodes.statement: Observe that for any fixed $r>0$, and given any random observation $G$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$, $\left|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}\setminus\mathcal{N}[\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2,r]\right| = n\prob{V_n\in \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}\setminus\mathcal{N}[\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2,r]\given \ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}=G}$, where we recall that $V_n$ denotes a typical vertex. Therefore, it is enough to show that for any $\varepsilon>0$, $r= r(\varepsilon)$ can be chosen large enough, such that $$\prob{V_n\in \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}\setminus\mathcal{N}[\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2,r]\given \ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}= G}\ensuremath{\xrightarrow{\mathbbm{P}}} \varepsilon'<\varepsilon, \quad \text{as}\quad n\to\infty.$$
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the conditional probability that a typical vertex lies far from the 2-core.

nodes.name: Local event approximation
nodes.statement: However, it is challenging to obtain the latter probability. For this reason, we will use the local event approximation technique, a key element in the study of sparse random graphs \cite{RGCN1,RGCN2,JLR00,BJM07,J08,BJR07}. In particular, our results for the configuration model mirror the ones proved in~\cite{BJR07} in the context of inhomogeneous random graphs. Roughly speaking, the crucial idea is based upon two observations:
nodes.statement_short: Use the local event approximation technique.

nodes.name: (i) Branching-process coupling
nodes.statement: The local neighborhood of a typical vertex resembles a branching process, i.e., with high probability, the breadth-first-search (BFS) exploration starting from $V_n$ up to suitable depth can be coupled with a branching process. This is formally stated in Proposition~\ref{prop-coupling}.
nodes.statement_short: Local neighborhoods couple with a branching process (Proposition 4.8).

nodes.name: (ii) Nearness to the 2-core is local
nodes.statement: Looking at the local neighborhood of $V_n$ up to suitable distance, it can be determined whether $V_n$ is near the 2-core. More specifically, the event that $V_n$ is within the $r$ neighborhood of the 2-core, is asymptotically `equivalent' to the event that for some $L_n \to \infty$, there exists two vertex disjoint paths of length $L_n$ from a vertex within the $r$ neighborhood of $V_n$. This fact is later formalized in Lemma~\ref{lem:loc-event-approx}. \end{enumerate} The proof follows once we have these ingredients in place.
nodes.statement_short: Being near the 2-core is approximated by a local event (Lemma 4.9).

nodes.name: Branching process X and size-biased degree D*
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathcal{X}$ the branching process with initial distribution $D$ and progeny distribution $D^*-1$, where $D$ is the limiting random variable as in Assumption~\ref{assumption1}, and $D^*$ follows the size-biased distribution of $D$, i.e., $$\prob{D^*=j}= \frac{j\ \prob{D=j}}{\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D]}, \quad j\geq 1.$$

nodes.name: Survival probability of X equals eta
nodes.statement: Note that the survival probability of $\mathcal{X}$ is given by $\eta$, as in~\eqref{defn:eta} (cf.~\cite{JL09}).

nodes.name: Generation sizes Z_l and BFS layer sizes Z_l(v)
nodes.statement: The number of offspring of $\mathcal{X}$ in generation $l$ is denoted by $\mathcal{Z}_l$, and the number of vertices at distance $l$ in the breadth-first neighborhood exploration tree (i.e.~the BFS tree) starting from vertex $v$ is denoted by $Z_l(v)$.

nodes.name: Events TC_r, LTC_r, DS_r and LDS_r
nodes.statement: Furthermore, define the following events: \begin{enumerate}[{\normalfont (a)}] \item $\mathrm{TC}_r(v)$: the vertex $v$ is within distance $r$ of the 2-core of $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}$, \item $\mathrm{LTC}_r(v,L)$: there exists a vertex $v'$ at distance $t$ of $v$, $t\leq r$, with two vertex disjoint paths of length $L$ starting at $v'$ which join $v'$ to the vertices at distance $t+L$ from $v$. \item $\mathrm{DS}_r$: the branching process $\mathcal{X}$ has a progeny within the first $r$ generations that has two children, both of which survive till infinity. \item $\mathrm{LDS}_r(L)$: the branching process $\mathcal{X}$ has a progeny within the first $r$ generations that has two children surviving further $L$ generations. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Events that v is within distance r of the 2-core, its local proxy, and the branching-process analogues.

nodes.name: Local weak coupling of neighborhoods with branching processes
nodes.statement: Let $\{\mathcal{Z}^1_l\}_{l\geq 1}, \{\mathcal{Z}^2_l\}_{l\geq 1}$ be two independent copies of $\{\mathcal{Z}_l\}_{l\geq 1}$, and $V_n$, $W_n$ be two independent typical vertices of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$. There exists $(L_n)_{n\geq 1}$ such that $L_n\to \infty$, and a coupling $\big((\hat{Z}^1_l, \hat{Z}^2_l), (\hat{\mathcal{Z}}^1_l,\hat{\mathcal{Z}}^2_l)\big)_{l=1}^{L_n}$ of $\big((Z_l(V_n), Z_l(W_n)), (\mathcal{Z}^1_l,\mathcal{Z}^2_l)\big)_{l=1}^{L_n}$ such that \begin{equation} \lim_{n\to\infty}\prob{\exists\ l\leq L_n: (\hat{Z}^1_l, \hat{Z}^2_l)\neq (\hat{\mathcal{Z}}^1_l,\hat{\mathcal{Z}}^2_l)}=0. \end{equation}
nodes.origin_citation: van der Hofstad, Random Graphs and Complex Networks Vol. 2, Proposition 5.4
nodes.statement_short: BFS layers from two typical vertices can be coupled to two independent branching processes up to a growing depth L_n.
nodes.label: prop-coupling

nodes.name: Coupling of neighborhoods with branching processes
nodes.statement: \lim_{n\to\infty}\prob{\exists\ l\leq L_n: (\hat{Z}^1_l, \hat{Z}^2_l)\neq (\hat{\mathcal{Z}}^1_l,\hat{\mathcal{Z}}^2_l)}=0.
nodes.origin_citation: van der Hofstad, Random Graphs and Complex Networks Vol. 2, Proposition 5.4
nodes.label: eq:coupling

nodes.name: Local event approximation of being near the 2-core
nodes.statement: Let $(L_n)_{n\geq 1}$ be such that $L_n\to\infty$ and $L_n/\log(n)\to 0$. Then, for any fixed $r\geq 1$, $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\prob{\mathrm{TC}_r(V_n)\ \Delta\ \mathrm{LTC}_r(V_n,L_n)}= 0.$$
conclusions: $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\prob{\mathrm{TC}_r(V_n)\ \Delta\ \mathrm{LTC}_r(V_n,L_n)}= 0.$$
nodes.statement_short: Being within distance r of the 2-core is asymptotically equivalent to the local two-long-disjoint-paths event.
nodes.label: lem:loc-event-approx

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.7
nodes.statement: Fix any $r>0$. Observe that for any $L_n$ such that $L_n\to\infty$, \begin{equation*} \lim_{n\to\infty}\prob{\mathrm{LDS}_r(L_n)}=\prob{\mathrm{DS}_r}. \end{equation*} Furthermore, choose $L_n^{(1)}$ according to Proposition~\ref{prop-coupling}, and $L_n^{(2)}$ such that Lemma~\ref{lem:loc-event-approx} holds. nodes.statement_short: As for Lemma 4.7: local approximation of the 2-core degree event plus coupling gives mean convergence and vanishing variance.

nodes.name: Similar to Lemma 4.7
nodes.statement: The proof follows using similar arguments as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:small-hanging-trees}.
nodes.statement_short: Follow the proof of Lemma 4.7.

nodes.statement: Having proved the local event approximation in Section~\ref{sec:local_approx}, the rest of the proof is similar to~\cite{BJR07}, and will be sketched briefly for completeness.
nodes.statement_short: The rest follows Bollobas-Janson-Riordan and is sketched.

nodes.name: Pairing probability
nodes.statement: For any subset $A \subset \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2$, we define $\bar{A} = \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2 \backslash A$. Further, recall that for $A \subset \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2$, we denote the half-edges incident to the vertices in $A$ by $S(A)$. For a set of half-edges $S$, denote by $p(S;\Mtilde{\bld{d}})$ the probability that the half-edges of $S$ are paired among each other in $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2$, conditional on~$\Mtilde{\bld{d}}$. Using the fact that the half-edges of $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2$ form a uniform perfect matching conditional on the degrees, we obtain \begin{equation} p(S;\Mtilde{\bld{d}}) = \frac{(|S| -1) !! (2m_2 - |S| - 1) !!}{(2m_2-1)!!} \leq \frac{1}{ \binom{m_2}{|S|/2 }}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Probability that a set of half-edges pairs internally.

nodes.name: Probability that half-edges in S pair among themselves
nodes.label: expr-p-S

nodes.name: Bad partitions
nodes.statement: A partition $A, \bar{A}$ of $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2$ is called $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-\emph{bad} if $|A|, | \bar{A}| \geq \varepsilon n$, and there is a subset $S\subset S(A)$ with $|S(A) \setminus S| \leq \delta n$ such that all the half-edges in $S$ are paired with each other during the random matching of the half-edges. Let $\Gamma_n$ denote the number of bad partitions of $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2$. Thus, \begin{align} \ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}_{\Mtilde{\bld{d}}}[\Gamma_n] \leq \sum_{ A \subset \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2 : |A|, |\bar{A}| \geq \varepsilon n } \sum_{S \subset S(A): |S(A)\backslash S| \leq \delta n} p(S;\Mtilde{\bld{d}}), \end{align} where $\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}_{\bld{\tilde{d}}}[\cdot]$ denotes the conditional expectation given the degree sequence of $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2$ to be $\Mtilde{\bld{d}}$. We need to show that for all $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon)>0$, such that $\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}_{\Mtilde{\bld{d}}}[\Gamma_n]\to 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Define bad partitions and bound their expected number by a double sum.

nodes.name: First moment bound on number of bad partitions
nodes.statement: \ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}_{\Mtilde{\bld{d}}}[\Gamma_n] \leq \sum_{ A \subset \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2 : |A|, |\bar{A}| \geq \varepsilon n } \sum_{S \subset S(A): |S(A)\backslash S| \leq \delta n} p(S;\Mtilde{\bld{d}}),
nodes.label: eq:firstmoment

nodes.name: Lower bound using degree-3 vertices
nodes.statement: We first derive a lower bound on $\binom{m_2}{|S|/2}$. Observe that each vertex in $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2$ has degree at least $2$, and thus, $|S(A)|/2 \geq |A|$ and $m_2 - |S(A)|/2 \geq |\bar{A}|$, where for the second inequality we have used the fact that $2m_2 -|S(A)| = S(\bar{A})$. Note that for a supercritical $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$, $\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D(D-2)]>0$, and Assumption~\ref{assumption1}.\ref{assumption1-3} thus implies $\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}(D\geq 3) >0$. Therefore, by Claim~\ref{claim:deg-dist-2core}, there exists $\varepsilon_1>0$ such that the proportion of degree 3 vertices in $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2$ is at least $\varepsilon_1 n$ with high probability. Fix such an $\varepsilon_1>0$, and let $\mathcal{A}_n$ denote the event that the proportion of degree 3 vertices in $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}^2$ is at least $\varepsilon_1 n$. Note that on $\mathcal{A}_n$, one of the parts among $A$ and $\bar{A}$ contains at least $\varepsilon_1n/2$ degree three vertices. Consequently, either $|S(A) |/2 \geq |A| + \varepsilon_1 n / 4$ or $ m_2 - |S(A)|/2 \geq |\bar{A}| + \varepsilon_1 n/4$ on $\mathcal{A}_n$. Using these bounds, and the fact that $|A|, |\bar{A}| \geq \varepsilon n$, it follows that \begin{align} \binom{m_2}{|S(A)|/2} \geq \exp(4an) \binom{n_2}{|A|} , \nonumber \end{align} for some $a>0$ chosen as a function of $\varepsilon, \varepsilon_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Many degree-3 core vertices give an exponential gain in the binomial lower bound.

nodes.name: Lower bound for S
nodes.statement: Moreover, for any partitions $A,\bar{A}$ we have $|S(A) \backslash S| \leq \delta n$, and $\delta$ can be chosen small enough such that \begin{align} \binom{m_2}{|S|/2 } \geq \exp(3an) \binom{n_2}{|A|}, \nonumber \end{align}which gives the requisite lower bound.
nodes.statement_short: Small delta keeps the exponential gain for S.

nodes.name: Counting choices
nodes.statement: To derive an upper bound on the number of possible choices for $A$ and $S$ in~\eqref{eq:firstmoment}, we note that given $|A|=a_0$, there are $\binom{n_2}{a_0}$ ways of choosing $A$. Also, given $A$, there are at most $\binom{2 m_2 }{\delta n}$ choices for $S(A)\setminus S$ such that $|S(A)\backslash S| \leq \delta n$. Plugging these estimates back into \eqref{eq:firstmoment} yields \begin{align} \ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}_{\bld{\tilde{d}}}[\Gamma_n] \leq \sum_{ \varepsilon n \leq a_0 \leq n_2 - \varepsilon n} \binom{n_2}{a_0} \binom{2m_2}{\delta n} \binom{n_2}{a_0}^{-1} \exp(-3an) \quad \text{on } \mathcal{A}_n. \nonumber \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Count choices of A and S and plug into the first moment.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus, for a small enough choice of $\delta>0$, it follows that \begin{equation*} \ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}_{\bld{\tilde{d}}}[\Gamma_n]\to 0\quad \text{on } \mathcal{A}_n, \quad\text{and}\quad \ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}(\mathcal{A}_n^c) \to 0. \end{equation*} This completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem-epsilon-delta-2-core}.
nodes.statement_short: For small delta the expected number of bad partitions vanishes.

nodes.name: Intermediate component
nodes.statement: A component $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (i)}$ for $i\geq 2$ (i.e., except the largest component) will be called an \emph{intermediate component} if $|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (i)}|>L_n$ for some $L_n\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Mass of large non-giant components Q_n(L)
nodes.statement: For any $L>0$, define \begin{equation} Q_n(L):=\sum_{i\geq 2}|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (i)}|\ind{|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (i)}| \geq L}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Mass of intermediate components Q_n(L)
nodes.statement: Q_n(L):=\sum_{i\geq 2}|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (i)}|\ind{|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (i)}| \geq L}.

nodes.name: Component of a vertex C(v)
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathscr{C}(v)$, the component in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$ containing the vertex $v$.

nodes.name: Small number of vertices in intermediate components
nodes.statement: For any $\varepsilon >0$, there exists $K=K(\varepsilon)$, such that \begin{equation} \limsup_{n\to\infty}\prob{V_n\notin \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}, |\mathscr{C}(V_n)|>K}<\varepsilon. \end{equation} Consequently, for any $L_n$ such that $L_n\to\infty$, as $n\to\infty$, \begin{equation} \frac{\expt{Q_n(L_n)}}{n}\to 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Few vertices lie in large non-giant components: P(V_n outside giant with component > K) is small, and E[Q_n(L_n)]/n tends to 0.
nodes.label: lem:small-no-giant

nodes.name: Few vertices in large non-giant components
nodes.statement: \limsup_{n\to\infty}\prob{V_n\notin \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}, |\mathscr{C}(V_n)|>K}<\varepsilon.
nodes.label: CVn-small

nodes.name: Vanishing mean of Q_n(L_n)/n
nodes.statement: \frac{\expt{Q_n(L_n)}}{n}\to 0.
nodes.label: eq:no-giant-small

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.10
nodes.statement: Fix any $K\geq 1$. Recall from Theorem~\ref{thm:JL09} that \begin{equation} \prob{V_n\in \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}} =\prob{\mathscr{C}(V_n)=\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}}\to \prob{|\mathcal{X}|=\infty}. \end{equation} Now, based on the information about the $K$-neighborhood of $V_n$, it can be exactly determined whether the event $\{|\mathscr{C}(V_n)|>K\}$ has occurred or not. Therefore, using Proposition~\ref{prop-coupling}, we have \begin{equation} \prob{|\mathscr{C}(V_n)|\leq K} = \prob{|\mathcal{X}|\leq K}+o(1). \end{equation} Combining \eqref{giant-prob} and \eqref{giant-large} yields \begin{equation} \begin{split} \prob{V_n\notin \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}, |\mathscr{C}(V_n)|>K} =\prob{|\mathcal{X}|\in (K,\infty)}+o(1), \end{split} \end{equation} and hence \eqref{CVn-small} follows. To see \eqref{eq:no-giant-small}, notice that by \eqref{CVn-small}, \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \frac{1}{n} \expt{Q_n(L_n)}&=\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}\bigg[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\geq 2}|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (i)}|\ind{|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (i)} |> L_n}\bigg]\\ &=\frac{1}{n}\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}\bigg[\sum_{v\in [n] }\ind{|\mathscr{C}(v) |> L_n}\bigg]=\prob{V_n\notin\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)},|\mathscr{C}(V_n)|>L_n}\to 0. \end{split} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Compare giant membership and component-size events of a typical vertex with the branching process via Theorem 2.1 and Proposition 4.8.

nodes.name: Giant membership
nodes.statement: Fix any $K\geq 1$. Recall from Theorem~\ref{thm:JL09} that \begin{equation} \prob{V_n\in \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}} =\prob{\mathscr{C}(V_n)=\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}}\to \prob{|\mathcal{X}|=\infty}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: A typical vertex is in the giant with probability tending to the survival probability.

nodes.name: Probability a typical vertex lies in the giant
nodes.statement: \prob{V_n\in \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}} =\prob{\mathscr{C}(V_n)=\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}}\to \prob{|\mathcal{X}|=\infty}.
nodes.label: giant-prob

nodes.name: Small components via coupling
nodes.statement: Now, based on the information about the $K$-neighborhood of $V_n$, it can be exactly determined whether the event $\{|\mathscr{C}(V_n)|>K\}$ has occurred or not. Therefore, using Proposition~\ref{prop-coupling}, we have \begin{equation} \prob{|\mathscr{C}(V_n)|\leq K} = \prob{|\mathcal{X}|\leq K}+o(1). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Component size at most K is determined locally, so coupling gives its probability.

nodes.name: Component size via branching process
nodes.statement: \prob{|\mathscr{C}(V_n)|\leq K} = \prob{|\mathcal{X}|\leq K}+o(1).
nodes.label: giant-large

nodes.name: First claim
nodes.statement: Combining \eqref{giant-prob} and \eqref{giant-large} yields \begin{equation} \begin{split} \prob{V_n\notin \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}, |\mathscr{C}(V_n)|>K} =\prob{|\mathcal{X}|\in (K,\infty)}+o(1), \end{split} \end{equation} and hence \eqref{CVn-small} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Subtract to get the probability of a large non-giant component.

nodes.name: Probability of large non-giant component of V_n
nodes.statement: \begin{split} \prob{V_n\notin \mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}, |\mathscr{C}(V_n)|>K} =\prob{|\mathcal{X}|\in (K,\infty)}+o(1), \end{split}

nodes.name: Second claim
nodes.statement: To see \eqref{eq:no-giant-small}, notice that by \eqref{CVn-small}, \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \frac{1}{n} \expt{Q_n(L_n)}&=\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}\bigg[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\geq 2}|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (i)}|\ind{|\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (i)} |> L_n}\bigg]\\ &=\frac{1}{n}\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}\bigg[\sum_{v\in [n] }\ind{|\mathscr{C}(v) |> L_n}\bigg]=\prob{V_n\notin\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)},|\mathscr{C}(V_n)|>L_n}\to 0. \end{split} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite E[Q_n(L_n)]/n as a typical-vertex probability that vanishes.

nodes.name: Sequential construction of the configuration model by coalescing degree-one vertices
nodes.statement: \normalfont Consider a given degree sequence $\bld{d}$ on vertex set $[n]$. Recall that $\ell_n = \sum_i d_i$ is the sum of the degrees. First $n_0$ isolated vertices are assigned their vertex labels. The algorithm below generates the random topology induced by the vertices of degree one or larger. \begin{enumerate}[(S1)] \item Initially there are $\ell_n$ degree one vertices labeled $v(1),\dots,v(\ell_n)$, each with an attached half-edge. Call these the set of \emph{red} vertices. Construct a uniform matching of these $\ell_n$ half-edges. Denote the corresponding graph by $\mathcal{G}(0)$, and set $V(0)=\emptyset$. Also, take any permutation of the index set $\{i\in [n]:d_i>1\}$ of all vertices of degree more than one, and denote it by $\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\ldots,\sigma_{\hat{n}}\}$, where $\hat{n}=n-n_0-n_1$. \item At step $t+1$, $0\leq t\leq \hat{n}-1$, choose $d_{\sigma_t}$ degree one vertices from the graph $\mathcal{G}(t)$ uniformly at random independently of the perfect matching, and coalesce them into a single \emph{black} vertex with index $\sigma_t$. Let $\mathcal{G}(t+1)$ be the new modified graph, and set $V(t+1)=V(t)\cup \{\sigma_t\}$. See Figure~\ref{fig:explosion} for an illustration of this step. \item After $\hat{n}^{\mathrm{th}}$ step, when all indices $i$ with $d_i>1$ are exhausted, label all the degree one vertices at random, independently of (S1) and (S2). \end{enumerate}
input: a given degree sequence $\bld{d}$ on vertex set $[n]$
output: the random topology induced by the vertices of degree one or larger
nodes.statement_short: Start from a uniform matching of l_n degree-one vertices and repeatedly coalesce d_v of them into a vertex v, labelling the rest at the end.
nodes.label: algo-CM

nodes.name: Label isolated vertices
nodes.statement: First $n_0$ isolated vertices are assigned their vertex labels.
nodes.statement_short: Assign labels to the degree-zero vertices.

nodes.name: (S1) Initial matching
nodes.statement: Initially there are $\ell_n$ degree one vertices labeled $v(1),\dots,v(\ell_n)$, each with an attached half-edge. Call these the set of \emph{red} vertices. Construct a uniform matching of these $\ell_n$ half-edges. Denote the corresponding graph by $\mathcal{G}(0)$, and set $V(0)=\emptyset$. Also, take any permutation of the index set $\{i\in [n]:d_i>1\}$ of all vertices of degree more than one, and denote it by $\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\ldots,\sigma_{\hat{n}}\}$, where $\hat{n}=n-n_0-n_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Match l_n red degree-one vertices uniformly and fix an order of high-degree indices.

nodes.name: Red vertices
nodes.statement: Initially there are $\ell_n$ degree one vertices labeled $v(1),\dots,v(\ell_n)$, each with an attached half-edge. Call these the set of \emph{red} vertices.
nodes.statement_short: Create l_n red degree-one vertices.

nodes.name: Uniform matching
nodes.statement: Construct a uniform matching of these $\ell_n$ half-edges.
nodes.statement_short: Pair the half-edges uniformly.

nodes.name: Initial graph
nodes.statement: Denote the corresponding graph by $\mathcal{G}(0)$, and set $V(0)=\emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: Set G(0) and V(0).

nodes.name: Order high-degree vertices
nodes.statement: Also, take any permutation of the index set $\{i\in [n]:d_i>1\}$ of all vertices of degree more than one, and denote it by $\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\ldots,\sigma_{\hat{n}}\}$, where $\hat{n}=n-n_0-n_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix an ordering of vertices of degree more than one.

nodes.name: (S2) Coalescence loop
nodes.statement: At step $t+1$, $0\leq t\leq \hat{n}-1$, choose $d_{\sigma_t}$ degree one vertices from the graph $\mathcal{G}(t)$ uniformly at random independently of the perfect matching, and coalesce them into a single \emph{black} vertex with index $\sigma_t$. Let $\mathcal{G}(t+1)$ be the new modified graph, and set $V(t+1)=V(t)\cup \{\sigma_t\}$. See Figure~\ref{fig:explosion} for an illustration of this step.
nodes.statement_short: For each high-degree vertex, merge d_v random degree-one vertices into one black vertex.

nodes.name: Choose and coalesce
nodes.statement: At step $t+1$, $0\leq t\leq \hat{n}-1$, choose $d_{\sigma_t}$ degree one vertices from the graph $\mathcal{G}(t)$ uniformly at random independently of the perfect matching, and coalesce them into a single \emph{black} vertex with index $\sigma_t$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick d_v degree-one vertices uniformly and merge them into a black vertex.

nodes.name: Update graph
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{G}(t+1)$ be the new modified graph, and set $V(t+1)=V(t)\cup \{\sigma_t\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Record the new graph and vertex set.

nodes.name: (S3) Label degree-one vertices
nodes.statement: After $\hat{n}^{\mathrm{th}}$ step, when all indices $i$ with $d_i>1$ are exhausted, label all the degree one vertices at random, independently of (S1) and (S2).
nodes.statement_short: Randomly label remaining degree-one vertices.

nodes.name: Justification of Lemma 4.11
nodes.statement: Note that the vertex index assignment process is independent of the initial perfect matching, and therefore, at any time step $t$, $\mathcal{G}(t)$ is a configuration model given its degree sequence. The algorithm, thus indeed produces a configuration model with degree sequence $\bld{d}$ in the end. This is formally stated in Lemma~\ref{lem:distn-alt-cons}.
nodes.statement_short: Index assignment is independent of the uniform matching, so every intermediate graph is a configuration model given its degrees.

nodes.name: Independence of labelling
nodes.statement: Note that the vertex index assignment process is independent of the initial perfect matching, and therefore, at any time step $t$, $\mathcal{G}(t)$ is a configuration model given its degree sequence.
nodes.statement_short: Labels are independent of the matching, so G(t) is a CM given its degrees.

nodes.name: Final graph
nodes.statement: The algorithm, thus indeed produces a configuration model with degree sequence $\bld{d}$ in the end. This is formally stated in Lemma~\ref{lem:distn-alt-cons}.
nodes.statement_short: Hence the final graph is CM_n(d).

nodes.name: Black subgraph is frozen
nodes.statement: Also, notice that at any time step $t$, the subgraph in $\mathcal{G}(t)$ induced by the set of black vertices remains fixed till the formation of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$.

nodes.name: Intermediate graphs of Algorithm 1 are configuration models
nodes.statement: For all $t\geq 0$, $\mathcal{G}(t)$ is a configuration model given its degree sequence. In particular, the final graph is distributed as \ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}.
conclusions: $\mathcal{G}(t)$ is a configuration model given its degree sequence.
the final graph is distributed as \ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}.
nodes.label: lem:distn-alt-cons

nodes.name: Order of index assignment in Algorithm 1
nodes.statement: {\normalfont In Algorithm~\ref{algo-CM}, the indices corresponding to the vertices with degrees at most one are assigned at the final step (S3). It is worthwhile to note that this is not strictly necessary in order for the algorithm to work. In particular, since the uniform matching is created independent of the index assignments, any assignment ordering produces $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$ in the end. In the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:loc-event-approx} below, however, we will require the stated order of indexing the vertices. }

nodes.name: Graph sequence G^v(t)
nodes.statement: Fix any vertex $v$ of degree at least 2, and any permutation $\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\ldots,\sigma_{\hat{n}}\}$ of the set $\{i\in [n]:d_i>1\}$ such that $\sigma_{\hat{n}}=v$. Denote the sequence of graphs constructed in Algorithm~\ref{algo-CM} by $\{\mathcal{G}^v(t)\}_{t\geq 0}$, i.e., $\mathcal{G}^v(t)$ denotes the graph at the $t^{\mathrm{th}}$ step.
nodes.statement_short: Run Algorithm 1 with v created last and call the resulting graphs G^v(t).

nodes.name: Maximum degree is o(sqrt n)
nodes.statement: For any degree sequence satisfying Assumptions~\ref{assumption1}.\ref{assumption1-1},~and~\ref{assumption1}.\ref{assumption1-2}, the maximum degree $d_{\max}$ is $o(\sqrt{n})$.
conclusions: the maximum degree $d_{\max}$ is $o(\sqrt{n})$
nodes.label: lem:maxdeg

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.12
nodes.statement: For each fixed $K\geq 1$, $\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D_n^2\ind{D_n\leq K}] \to \ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D^2\ind{D\leq K}],$ and consequently, $\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D_n^2\ind{D_n>K}] \to \ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D^2\ind{D>K}].$ Thus, $$\lim_{K\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D_n^2\ind{D_n> K}]= \lim_{K\to\infty}\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D^2\ind{D>K}] =0.$$ Moreover, observe that \begin{equation*} \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{d_{\max}^2}{n}\leq \limsup_{n\to\infty}\Big[ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i:d_i>K}d_i^2 + \frac{K^2}{n} \Big] = \limsup_{n\to\infty}\expt{D_n^2\ind{D_n>K}}. \end{equation*} Since the left side of the above inequality does not depend on $K$, it follows that \begin{equation*} \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{d_{\max}^2}{n}\leq \limsup_{K\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\expt{D_n^2\ind{D_n>K}}=0. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Uniform integrability of D_n^2 makes the tail second moment vanish, which bounds d_max^2/n.

nodes.name: Vanishing tail second moment
nodes.statement: For each fixed $K\geq 1$, $\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D_n^2\ind{D_n\leq K}] \to \ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D^2\ind{D\leq K}],$ and consequently, $\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D_n^2\ind{D_n>K}] \to \ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D^2\ind{D>K}].$ Thus, $$\lim_{K\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D_n^2\ind{D_n> K}]= \lim_{K\to\infty}\ensuremath{\mathbbm{E}}[D^2\ind{D>K}] =0.$$
nodes.statement_short: Second-moment convergence gives vanishing tail moments.

nodes.name: Bound d_max^2/n
nodes.statement: Moreover, observe that \begin{equation*} \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{d_{\max}^2}{n}\leq \limsup_{n\to\infty}\Big[ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i:d_i>K}d_i^2 + \frac{K^2}{n} \Big] = \limsup_{n\to\infty}\expt{D_n^2\ind{D_n>K}}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound d_max^2/n by the tail second moment.

nodes.name: Let K grow

nodes.statement: In the proof we will make use of the path counting techniques as in~\cite{J09b, BDHS17}.
nodes.statement_short: Use path counting.

nodes.name: Choose kappa
nodes.statement: Define $\ell_n':=\ell_n-4L_n+1$. Note that due to Assumption~\ref{assumption1}.\ref{assumption1-2}, a constant $\kappa >1$ can be chosen such that \begin{equation} \frac{1}{\ell_n'}\sum_{i\in [n]}d_i(d_i-1)\leq \kappa \quad\mbox{for all}\quad n\geq 1. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the normalized second factorial moment by kappa.

nodes.name: Choice of constant kappa
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{\ell_n'}\sum_{i\in [n]}d_i(d_i-1)\leq \kappa \quad\mbox{for all}\quad n\geq 1.

nodes.name: Count structures
nodes.statement: The event $\mathrm{C}(V_n,L_n,L_n)$ implies that there is a path $(V_n, x_1,x_2,\ldots, x_{l})$ of length $l \leq L_n$, and $x_{l}$ belongs to a cycle $(x_{l},x_{l+1},\ldots,x_{l+m-1})$ of length $m\leq L_n$, where the $x_i$'s are distinct. Fix some $V_n=v$. Then the number of structures with a path $(v, x_1,x_2,\ldots, x_l)$ and a cycle $(x_l,x_{l+1},\ldots,x_{l+m-1})$ is given by $$\bigg[d_v\bigg(\prod_{i=1}^{l-1}d_{x_i}(d_{x_i}-1)\bigg) d_{x_l}\bigg]\times \bigg[(d_{x_l}-1) \bigg(\prod_{i=l+1}^{l+m-1}d_{x_i}(d_{x_i}-1)\bigg)(d_{x_l}-2) \bigg],$$ where the first term in the product is due to the number of ways the path can be formed, and the second is due to the cycle. Furthermore, each of these specific configurations has probability $[(\ell_n-1)(\ell_n-3)\dots(\ell_n-2l-2m+1)]^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Count path-plus-cycle configurations and their probability.

nodes.name: Conditional bound
nodes.statement: Therefore, \begin{equation} \begin{split} &\prob{\mathrm{C}(V_n,L_n,L_n)\given V_n=v}\\ & \hspace{1cm}\leq \sum_{l,m\leq L_n}\sum_{x_1,\dots,x_{l+m-1}}\dfrac{(d_{x_1}-2)d_v\prod_{i=1}^{l+m-1}d_{x_i}(d_{x_i}-1)}{(\ell_n-1)(\ell_n-3)\dots(\ell_n-2l-2m+1)}\\ & \hspace{1cm}\leq \sum_{l,m\leq L_n}\frac{1}{(\ell_n')^{m+l}} \bigg(\sum_{i\in [n]}d_i(d_i-1)\bigg)^{l+m-2}d_v\sum_{i\in [n]}d_i(d_i-1)(d_i-2) \\ & \hspace{1cm}\leq \sum_{l,m\leq L_n} \bigg(\frac{1}{\ell'_n}\sum_{i\in [n]}d_i(d_i-1)\bigg)^{l+m-2}d_v\frac{d_{\max}}{\ell_n'}\frac{1}{\ell_n'}\sum_{i\in [n]}d_i(d_i-1)\\ & \hspace{1cm}\leq \sum_{l,m\leq L_n} \bigg(\frac{1}{\ell'_n}\sum_{i\in [n]}d_i(d_i-1)\bigg)^{l+m-1} d_v\frac{d_{\max}}{\ell_n'} \quad \leq\ K \frac{d_v\kappa ^{2L_n}}{\sqrt{n}} \end{split} \end{equation} for some constant $K>0$ where in the final step we have used \eqref{eq:choice-k} and Lemma~\ref{lem:maxdeg}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the conditional probability by K d_v kappa^{2L_n}/sqrt(n).

nodes.name: Idea of the proof of Theorem 3.2 (ii)
nodes.statement: The proof for the supercritical case builds upon the following idea: the fact that a graph has small Max-Cut implies that deletion of a small number of edges can make the graph bipartite. When the graph is supercritical, deletion of a small number of edges can still leave it supercritical. In that case, if one can show that the probability of the latter supercritical graph being bipartite is small, then the original supercritical cannot have a small Max-Cut.
nodes.statement_short: Idea: small Max-Cut deficit means a few deletions make the graph bipartite, but a still-supercritical graph is rarely bipartite.

Also, observe that if $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}(t(\varepsilon))$ is non-bipartite, then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$ will also be non-bipartite. Indeed, if $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}(t(\varepsilon))$ is non-bipartite, then it must contain an odd cycle of black nodes, and the process of merging degree one (red) vertices does not affect these existing cycles. Thus if there is an odd-length cycle in $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}(t(\varepsilon))$, that cycle will be present in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$ as well. nodes.name: Partition algorithm
nodes.statement: For $t\geq t(\varepsilon)$ we will now describe an algorithm for partitioning $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}(t)$ into two vertex-disjoint sets $H_1(t)$ and $H_2(t)$ in a coupled way. The sets $H_1(t)$ and $H_2(t)$ are such that if $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}(t)$ is bipartite, then these are the unique partite sets. For $i=1,2$, let $H_i^B(t)$ and $H_i^R(t)$ be the set of black and red vertices in $H_i(t)$, respectively. Also, let $R(t)$ and $R_P(t)$ denote the set of all red vertices and red pairs in $\mathcal{G}_n(t)$, respectively (recall that a pair is two degree one vertices joined with each other). With a little abuse of notation, we will also write $H_i^B(t)$, $R(t)$ etc.~to denote the cardinality of the respective sets. \begin{algo} \normalfont Initially consider the unique bipartition of $\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}(t(\varepsilon))$: $$\mathscr{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle (1)}(t(\varepsilon)) = H_1(t(\varepsilon))\sqcup H_2(t(\varepsilon)),\ \mathrm{say}.$$ At time step $t> t(\varepsilon)$, suppose two red vertices $v_1$ and $v_1$ are coalesced to form a new black vertex $v$ of degree 2. Then the sets $H_1(t)$ and $H_2(t)$ are updated according to the following rule: \begin{enumerate}[{\normalfont (i)}] \item If both $v_1, v_2\in H_i^R(t-1)$ for either $i=1$ or 2, then $$H_i(t)= \big(H_i(t-1)\setminus \{v_1,v_2\}\big)\cup \{v\},$$ and the other partition remains unchanged. \item If $v_1\in H_1^R(t-1)$ and $v_2\in R(t-1)\setminus (H_2^R(t-1)\cup H_1^R(t-1))$, then \begin{align*} H_1(t) &= \Big(H_1(t-1)\setminus \{v_1\}\Big) \cup\{v\}\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty \Big(\mathcal{N}[v_2,2k]\setminus \mathcal{N}[v_2,2k-1]\Big),\\ H_2(t) &= H_2(t-1)\bigcup_{k=0}^\infty \Big(\mathcal{N}[v_2,2k+1]\setminus \mathcal{N}[v_2,2k]\Big) \end{align*} where by convention, the zero neighborhood of a vertex is the vertex itself. \item If $v_1\in H_2^R(t-1)$ and $v_2\in R(t-1)\setminus (H_2^R(t-1)\cup H_1^R(t-1))$, then repeat Step (ii) above by interchanging the role of $H_1$ and $H_2$. \item If both $v_1, v_2\in R(t-1)\setminus (H_2^R(t-1)\cup H_1^R(t-1))$, then $H_i(t) = H_i(t-1)$, $i=1,2$. \item If $v_1\in H_1^R(t-1)$ and $ v_2\in H_2^R(t-1)$ or vice versa, then remove $v_1$ and $v_2$ from their respective sets, and add $v$ to $H_1(t)$ or $H_2(t)$ arbitrarily. \end{enumerate} \end{algo}
