nodes.name: Update rule at each step
nodes.statement: At time step $t> t(\varepsilon)$, suppose two red vertices $v_1$ and $v_1$ are coalesced to form a new black vertex $v$ of degree 2. Then the sets $H_1(t)$ and $H_2(t)$ are updated according to the following rule: \begin{enumerate}[{\normalfont (i)}] \item If both $v_1, v_2\in H_i^R(t-1)$ for either $i=1$ or 2, then $$H_i(t)= \big(H_i(t-1)\setminus \{v_1,v_2\}\big)\cup \{v\},$$ and the other partition remains unchanged. \item If $v_1\in H_1^R(t-1)$ and $v_2\in R(t-1)\setminus (H_2^R(t-1)\cup H_1^R(t-1))$, then \begin{align*} H_1(t) &= \Big(H_1(t-1)\setminus \{v_1\}\Big) \cup\{v\}\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty \Big(\mathcal{N}[v_2,2k]\setminus \mathcal{N}[v_2,2k-1]\Big),\\ H_2(t) &= H_2(t-1)\bigcup_{k=0}^\infty \Big(\mathcal{N}[v_2,2k+1]\setminus \mathcal{N}[v_2,2k]\Big) \end{align*} where by convention, the zero neighborhood of a vertex is the vertex itself. \item If $v_1\in H_2^R(t-1)$ and $v_2\in R(t-1)\setminus (H_2^R(t-1)\cup H_1^R(t-1))$, then repeat Step (ii) above by interchanging the role of $H_1$ and $H_2$. \item If both $v_1, v_2\in R(t-1)\setminus (H_2^R(t-1)\cup H_1^R(t-1))$, then $H_i(t) = H_i(t-1)$, $i=1,2$. \item If $v_1\in H_1^R(t-1)$ and $ v_2\in H_2^R(t-1)$ or vice versa, then remove $v_1$ and $v_2$ from their respective sets, and add $v$ to $H_1(t)$ or $H_2(t)$ arbitrarily.
nodes.statement_short: At each coalescence of two red vertices, update H_1, H_2 by cases.

nodes.name: (i) Same side
nodes.statement: If both $v_1, v_2\in H_i^R(t-1)$ for either $i=1$ or 2, then $$H_i(t)= \big(H_i(t-1)\setminus \{v_1,v_2\}\big)\cup \{v\},$$ and the other partition remains unchanged.
nodes.statement_short: Both in H_i: replace them by v in H_i.

nodes.name: (ii) Attach outside component to H_1
nodes.statement: If $v_1\in H_1^R(t-1)$ and $v_2\in R(t-1)\setminus (H_2^R(t-1)\cup H_1^R(t-1))$, then \begin{align*} H_1(t) &= \Big(H_1(t-1)\setminus \{v_1\}\Big) \cup\{v\}\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty \Big(\mathcal{N}[v_2,2k]\setminus \mathcal{N}[v_2,2k-1]\Big),\\ H_2(t) &= H_2(t-1)\bigcup_{k=0}^\infty \Big(\mathcal{N}[v_2,2k+1]\setminus \mathcal{N}[v_2,2k]\Big) \end{align*} where by convention, the zero neighborhood of a vertex is the vertex itself.
nodes.statement_short: Add v to H_1 and 2-color v_2's component accordingly.

nodes.name: (iii) Attach outside component to H_2
nodes.statement: If $v_1\in H_2^R(t-1)$ and $v_2\in R(t-1)\setminus (H_2^R(t-1)\cup H_1^R(t-1))$, then repeat Step (ii) above by interchanging the role of $H_1$ and $H_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric to (ii).

nodes.name: (iv) Both outside
nodes.statement: If both $v_1, v_2\in R(t-1)\setminus (H_2^R(t-1)\cup H_1^R(t-1))$, then $H_i(t) = H_i(t-1)$, $i=1,2$.
nodes.statement_short: No change.

nodes.name: (v) Opposite sides
nodes.statement: If $v_1\in H_1^R(t-1)$ and $ v_2\in H_2^R(t-1)$ or vice versa, then remove $v_1$ and $v_2$ from their respective sets, and add $v$ to $H_1(t)$ or $H_2(t)$ arbitrarily.
nodes.statement_short: Bipartiteness is broken; place v arbitrarily.

nodes.name: Monotonicity and case (v)
nodes.statement: Note that for $t_1<t_2$, $H_1^B(t_1)\subseteq H_1^B(t_2)$ and $H_2^B(t_1)\subseteq H_2^B(t_2)$. Also, if $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$ is bipartite, then $\mathcal{G}_n(t)$ must be bipartite for all $t>t(\varepsilon)$. In that case, Case (v) of Algorithm~\ref{algo:partition} should not occur, otherwise the bipartiteness will be lost.
nodes.statement_short: Black parts only grow; bipartiteness requires case (v) never to occur.

nodes.name: Claim 5
nodes.statement: We now claim that the number of red vertices in both partitions will become order $n$ at some time step after $t(\varepsilon)$. Afterwards we establish that if the claim is true, then the probability that Case (v) of Algorithm~\ref{algo:partition} will not occur is exponentially small. As a result, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$ is bipartite with exponentially small probability. \begin{claim} For sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta_1=\delta_1(\varepsilon)>0$ and $\delta_2=\delta_2(\varepsilon)>0$ such that \begin{equation} \prob{\forall\ t>t(\varepsilon),\ H_1^R(t)<\delta_1n\ \mbox{\rm or }H_2^R(t)<\delta_2n\vert\mathcal{G}_n(t(\varepsilon))} \leq \ensuremath{\mathrm{e}}^{-C_0n (1+\ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(1))}. \end{equation} \end{claim} \begin{claimproof} Note that since $\mathcal{G}_n(t(\varepsilon))$ is distributed as a configuration model, \cite[Theorem~2.3~(i)]{JL09} and Lemma~\ref{lem:num-pairs} respectively yields \begin{equation} \frac{H_1^R(t(\varepsilon))+H_2^R(t(\varepsilon))}{n} \ensuremath{\xrightarrow{\mathbbm{P}}} r(\varepsilon)>0\qquad\mathrm{and}\qquad \frac{R_P(t(\varepsilon))}{n}\ensuremath{\xrightarrow{\mathbbm{P}}} r_P(\varepsilon)>0. \end{equation} Due to~\eqref{eq:total-red-giant}, one of the sets $H_1^R(t(\varepsilon))$ or $H_2^R(t(\varepsilon))$ has atleast $r(\varepsilon) n/4$ red vertices with high probability. Without loss of generality, let the part be $H_1^R(t(\varepsilon))$. Since at each time step $t> t(\varepsilon)$ only degree 2 vertices are created, the set of red vertices can deplete by at most 2. Therefore, for $t^*(\varepsilon) = t(\varepsilon)+\min\{r(\varepsilon) n/8,\varepsilon\ell_n/2\}$, \begin{equation} \inf_{t(\varepsilon)\leq t\leq t^*(\varepsilon)} H^R_1(t)\geq\frac{r(\varepsilon)n}{8}=:\delta_1n. \end{equation} It is important to note that both $r(\varepsilon)$ and $r_P(\varepsilon)$ are bounded away from zero as $\varepsilon\to 0$. Thus $\delta_1$ remains positive even when $\varepsilon$ is chosen small enough. Recall from Algorithm~\ref{algo:partition}(ii) that during the time interval $[t(\varepsilon), t^*(\varepsilon)]$, $H_2^R$ increases by at least one if some red vertex in $H_1^R$ is coalesced with one of the vertices outside the set $H_1^R\cup H_2^R$, in particular, with one belonging to some red pair in $R_P$. Using \eqref{eq:delta1up}, at each time step the probability of the latter event, conditionally on $\mathcal{G}_n(t(\varepsilon))$, is atleast $$\frac{r(\varepsilon)n}{8}r_P(\varepsilon)n{n_1 + 2 n_2\choose 2}^{-1}\geq \delta_1 c_1(1+\ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(1)),$$ for some $c_1\in (0,1]$. Denote by $\mathcal{A}(t)$ the cumulative number of red vertices thus added to $H_2^R$ up to time $t$ starting from $t(\varepsilon)$. Observe that $\mathcal{A}(t)$ stochastically dominates a binomial random variable with $\min\{r(\varepsilon) n/8,\varepsilon\ell_n/2\}$ number of trials and the success probability atleast $\delta_1 c_1(1+\ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(1))$. Therefore, standard concentration inequalities for the binomial distribution \cite[Corollary 2.3]{JLR00} yields \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}(\mathcal{A}(t^*(\varepsilon))\leq \delta_2' n|\mathcal{G}_n(t(\varepsilon)))\leq \ensuremath{\mathrm{e}}^{-C_0'n (1+\ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(1))} \end{equation} for some suitable $\delta_2'>0$ and a constant $C_0'>0$. Further notice that some of the red vertices in $H_2^R(t)$ have been coalesced to form new black vertices during $[t(\varepsilon),t^*(\varepsilon)]$. This can occur if only if at the coalescence step both red vertices are selected from $H_2^R$, which occurs with probability at most ${H_2^R(t)\choose 2}/{n_1\choose 2}$. Denote the cumulative number of such coalesced red vertices up to time $t$ by $\mathcal{B}(t)$. Define $$\tau(\varepsilon):= \inf\{t\geq t(\varepsilon): H_2^R(t) \geq \delta_2'n/2\}\wedge t^*(\varepsilon).$$ Then observe that for $t\in [t(\varepsilon), \tau(\varepsilon)]$, the quantity $\mathcal{B}(t)$ is dominated by a binomial random variable with $\min\{r(\varepsilon) n/8,\varepsilon\ell_n/2\}$ number of trials and success probability at most $\delta_2' n/2n_1$. The mean of this binomial random variable is of the order at most $\varepsilon\delta_2'n$, which can be made arbitrarily small compared to $\delta_2'n$ by choosing $\varepsilon$ small enough. Therefore, standard concentration inequalities for the binomial distribution again imply that \begin{equation} \prob{\mathcal{B}(\tau(\varepsilon))\geq \delta_2'n/4\ \vert\ \mathcal{G}_n(t(\varepsilon)), \{H_1^R(t) \leq \delta_2'n,\forall\ t(\varepsilon) \leq t < \tau(\varepsilon)\}}\leq \ensuremath{\mathrm{e}}^{-C_0''n(1+\ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(1))} \end{equation} for some constant $C_0''>0$. Now set $\delta_1$ as above and $\delta_2 := \delta_2'/2$, and observe that $H_2^R(t) = H_2^R(t(\varepsilon))+\mathcal{A}(t)-2\mathcal{B}(t)$. Thus \eqref{eq:bound-deg-1-A} and \eqref{eq:bound-deg-1-B} yields that either the probability that the following will not occur is exponentially small \begin{align*} H_2^R(\tau(\varepsilon)) &= H_2^R(t(\varepsilon))+\mathcal{A}(\tau(\varepsilon))-2\mathcal{B}(\tau(\varepsilon))\geq \delta_2 n, \end{align*} or $H_2^R(t)>\delta_2n$ for some $t\in[t(\varepsilon), \tau(\varepsilon)]$. In either of the two cases, this completes the proof of Claim~\ref{claim:good-cut}. \end{claimproof}
nodes.statement_short: Claim 5: both partite sets get linearly many red vertices.

nodes.name: Both sides gain linearly many red vertices
nodes.statement: For sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta_1=\delta_1(\varepsilon)>0$ and $\delta_2=\delta_2(\varepsilon)>0$ such that \begin{equation} \prob{\forall\ t>t(\varepsilon),\ H_1^R(t)<\delta_1n\ \mbox{\rm or }H_2^R(t)<\delta_2n\vert\mathcal{G}_n(t(\varepsilon))} \leq \ensuremath{\mathrm{e}}^{-C_0n (1+\ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(1))}. \end{equation}
conclusions: there exists $\delta_1=\delta_1(\varepsilon)>0$ and $\delta_2=\delta_2(\varepsilon)>0$ such that \begin{equation} \prob{\forall\ t>t(\varepsilon),\ H_1^R(t)<\delta_1n\ \mbox{\rm or }H_2^R(t)<\delta_2n\vert\mathcal{G}_n(t(\varepsilon))} \leq \ensuremath{\mathrm{e}}^{-C_0n (1+\ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(1))}. \end{equation}
nodes.label: claim:good-cut

nodes.name: Both partite sets acquire many red vertices
nodes.statement: \prob{\forall\ t>t(\varepsilon),\ H_1^R(t)<\delta_1n\ \mbox{\rm or }H_2^R(t)<\delta_2n\vert\mathcal{G}_n(t(\varepsilon))} \leq \ensuremath{\mathrm{e}}^{-C_0n (1+\ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(1))}.

nodes.name: Linear red counts
nodes.statement: Note that since $\mathcal{G}_n(t(\varepsilon))$ is distributed as a configuration model, \cite[Theorem~2.3~(i)]{JL09} and Lemma~\ref{lem:num-pairs} respectively yields \begin{equation} \frac{H_1^R(t(\varepsilon))+H_2^R(t(\varepsilon))}{n} \ensuremath{\xrightarrow{\mathbbm{P}}} r(\varepsilon)>0\qquad\mathrm{and}\qquad \frac{R_P(t(\varepsilon))}{n}\ensuremath{\xrightarrow{\mathbbm{P}}} r_P(\varepsilon)>0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Giant red vertices and red pairs are linear by Janson-Luczak and Lemma 4.2.

nodes.name: Red vertices in giant and red pairs
nodes.statement: \frac{H_1^R(t(\varepsilon))+H_2^R(t(\varepsilon))}{n} \ensuremath{\xrightarrow{\mathbbm{P}}} r(\varepsilon)>0\qquad\mathrm{and}\qquad \frac{R_P(t(\varepsilon))}{n}\ensuremath{\xrightarrow{\mathbbm{P}}} r_P(\varepsilon)>0.
nodes.label: eq:total-red-giant

nodes.name: WLOG H_1 large
nodes.statement: Due to~\eqref{eq:total-red-giant}, one of the sets $H_1^R(t(\varepsilon))$ or $H_2^R(t(\varepsilon))$ has atleast $r(\varepsilon) n/4$ red vertices with high probability. Without loss of generality, let the part be $H_1^R(t(\varepsilon))$.
nodes.statement_short: One side has at least r(eps)n/4 red vertices; call it H_1.

nodes.name: H_1 stays large
nodes.statement: Since at each time step $t> t(\varepsilon)$ only degree 2 vertices are created, the set of red vertices can deplete by at most 2. Therefore, for $t^*(\varepsilon) = t(\varepsilon)+\min\{r(\varepsilon) n/8,\varepsilon\ell_n/2\}$, \begin{equation} \inf_{t(\varepsilon)\leq t\leq t^*(\varepsilon)} H^R_1(t)\geq\frac{r(\varepsilon)n}{8}=:\delta_1n. \end{equation} It is important to note that both $r(\varepsilon)$ and $r_P(\varepsilon)$ are bounded away from zero as $\varepsilon\to 0$. Thus $\delta_1$ remains positive even when $\varepsilon$ is chosen small enough.
nodes.statement_short: Red vertices deplete by at most 2 per step, so H_1^R stays above delta_1 n.

nodes.name: Lower bound on H_1^R over time window
nodes.statement: \inf_{t(\varepsilon)\leq t\leq t^*(\varepsilon)} H^R_1(t)\geq\frac{r(\varepsilon)n}{8}=:\delta_1n.
nodes.label: eq:delta1up

nodes.name: Growth probability of H_2
nodes.statement: Recall from Algorithm~\ref{algo:partition}(ii) that during the time interval $[t(\varepsilon), t^*(\varepsilon)]$, $H_2^R$ increases by at least one if some red vertex in $H_1^R$ is coalesced with one of the vertices outside the set $H_1^R\cup H_2^R$, in particular, with one belonging to some red pair in $R_P$. Using \eqref{eq:delta1up}, at each time step the probability of the latter event, conditionally on $\mathcal{G}_n(t(\varepsilon))$, is atleast $$\frac{r(\varepsilon)n}{8}r_P(\varepsilon)n{n_1 + 2 n_2\choose 2}^{-1}\geq \delta_1 c_1(1+\ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(1)),$$ for some $c_1\in (0,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Each step adds to H_2^R with probability at least delta_1 c_1.

nodes.name: Binomial domination for gains
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathcal{A}(t)$ the cumulative number of red vertices thus added to $H_2^R$ up to time $t$ starting from $t(\varepsilon)$. Observe that $\mathcal{A}(t)$ stochastically dominates a binomial random variable with $\min\{r(\varepsilon) n/8,\varepsilon\ell_n/2\}$ number of trials and the success probability atleast $\delta_1 c_1(1+\ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(1))$. Therefore, standard concentration inequalities for the binomial distribution \cite[Corollary 2.3]{JLR00} yields \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}(\mathcal{A}(t^*(\varepsilon))\leq \delta_2' n|\mathcal{G}_n(t(\varepsilon)))\leq \ensuremath{\mathrm{e}}^{-C_0'n (1+\ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(1))} \end{equation} for some suitable $\delta_2'>0$ and a constant $C_0'>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Gains dominate a binomial; Chernoff gives exponential concentration.

nodes.name: Concentration bound for A(t)
nodes.statement: \ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}(\mathcal{A}(t^*(\varepsilon))\leq \delta_2' n|\mathcal{G}_n(t(\varepsilon)))\leq \ensuremath{\mathrm{e}}^{-C_0'n (1+\ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(1))}
nodes.label: eq:bound-deg-1-A

nodes.name: Losses are small
nodes.statement: Further notice that some of the red vertices in $H_2^R(t)$ have been coalesced to form new black vertices during $[t(\varepsilon),t^*(\varepsilon)]$. This can occur if only if at the coalescence step both red vertices are selected from $H_2^R$, which occurs with probability at most ${H_2^R(t)\choose 2}/{n_1\choose 2}$. Denote the cumulative number of such coalesced red vertices up to time $t$ by $\mathcal{B}(t)$. Define $$\tau(\varepsilon):= \inf\{t\geq t(\varepsilon): H_2^R(t) \geq \delta_2'n/2\}\wedge t^*(\varepsilon).$$ Then observe that for $t\in [t(\varepsilon), \tau(\varepsilon)]$, the quantity $\mathcal{B}(t)$ is dominated by a binomial random variable with $\min\{r(\varepsilon) n/8,\varepsilon\ell_n/2\}$ number of trials and success probability at most $\delta_2' n/2n_1$. The mean of this binomial random variable is of the order at most $\varepsilon\delta_2'n$, which can be made arbitrarily small compared to $\delta_2'n$ by choosing $\varepsilon$ small enough. Therefore, standard concentration inequalities for the binomial distribution again imply that \begin{equation} \prob{\mathcal{B}(\tau(\varepsilon))\geq \delta_2'n/4\ \vert\ \mathcal{G}_n(t(\varepsilon)), \{H_1^R(t) \leq \delta_2'n,\forall\ t(\varepsilon) \leq t < \tau(\varepsilon)\}}\leq \ensuremath{\mathrm{e}}^{-C_0''n(1+\ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(1))} \end{equation} for some constant $C_0''>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Losses are dominated by a binomial with small mean.

nodes.name: Concentration bound for B(t)
nodes.statement: \prob{\mathcal{B}(\tau(\varepsilon))\geq \delta_2'n/4\ \vert\ \mathcal{G}_n(t(\varepsilon)), \{H_1^R(t) \leq \delta_2'n,\forall\ t(\varepsilon) \leq t < \tau(\varepsilon)\}}\leq \ensuremath{\mathrm{e}}^{-C_0''n(1+\ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(1))}
nodes.label: eq:bound-deg-1-B

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Now set $\delta_1$ as above and $\delta_2 := \delta_2'/2$, and observe that $H_2^R(t) = H_2^R(t(\varepsilon))+\mathcal{A}(t)-2\mathcal{B}(t)$. Thus \eqref{eq:bound-deg-1-A} and \eqref{eq:bound-deg-1-B} yields that either the probability that the following will not occur is exponentially small \begin{align*} H_2^R(\tau(\varepsilon)) &= H_2^R(t(\varepsilon))+\mathcal{A}(\tau(\varepsilon))-2\mathcal{B}(\tau(\varepsilon))\geq \delta_2 n, \end{align*} or $H_2^R(t)>\delta_2n$ for some $t\in[t(\varepsilon), \tau(\varepsilon)]$. In either of the two cases, this completes the proof of Claim~\ref{claim:good-cut}.
nodes.statement_short: Gains minus losses give H_2^R at least delta_2 n except with exponentially small probability.

nodes.name: Red sets stay large
nodes.statement: Let $t^{**}(\varepsilon):=\tau(\varepsilon)+(\delta_1\wedge\delta_2)n/4$. Observe that due to Claim~\ref{claim:good-cut} and the argument given above~\eqref{eq:delta1up}, \begin{equation} \inf_{\tau(\varepsilon)\leq t\leq t^{**}(\varepsilon)} H^R_i(t)\geq \frac{\delta_in}{4}\qquad i = 1,2. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Both red sets remain linear on a window after tau.

nodes.name: Lower bound on H_i^R after tau
nodes.statement: \inf_{\tau(\varepsilon)\leq t\leq t^{**}(\varepsilon)} H^R_i(t)\geq \frac{\delta_in}{4}\qquad i = 1,2.

nodes.name: Constant breaking probability
nodes.statement: Recall that while forming the degree 2 vertices from $\mathcal{G}_n(\tau(\varepsilon))$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$, the bipartiteness is lost if one red vertex is chosen from~$H_1^R$ and the other is chosen from~$H_2^R$. Therefore, for any $t\in[\tau(\varepsilon), t^{**}(\varepsilon)]$, \begin{align*} &\prob{\text{Bipartiteness is not preserved at time }t \vert \mathcal{G}_n(t(\varepsilon)),\ H_1^R(\tau(\varepsilon))\geq \delta_1n,\ H_2^R(\tau(\varepsilon))\geq \delta_2n}\\ &\geq \frac{\delta_1\delta_2n^2}{16{n_1 \choose 2}} = (1-c_0)(1+\ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(1)), \end{align*} for some $c_0\in (0,1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Each step breaks bipartiteness with probability bounded below.

nodes.name: Exponential bound
nodes.statement: Thus the probability that bipartiteness is preserved troughtout the time interval $[\tau(\varepsilon), t^{**}(\varepsilon)]$ given $\mathcal{G}_n(t(\varepsilon))$, $H_1^R(\tau(\varepsilon))\geq \delta_1n$, and $H_2^R(\tau(\varepsilon))\geq \delta_2n$ is upper bounded by $\exp(-C_0(1+\ensuremath{o_{\scriptscriptstyle\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}}}(1))n)$ for some constant $C_0>0$. The proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:prob-bipartite} is now complete.
nodes.statement_short: Surviving linearly many steps has exponentially small probability.

nodes.name: Small sets have small sum of squared degrees
nodes.statement: Under Assumption~\ref{assumption1}.\ref{assumption1-2}, given any $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon) >0$, such that for all sufficiently large $n$, the sum of squares of the degrees of \emph{any} collection of $\delta n$ vertices is at most~$\varepsilon n$, i.e. $\sum_{u\in U}d_i(d_i-1)<\varepsilon n$ uniformly over all subsets $U\subseteq [n]$ such that $|U|< \delta n$.
conclusions: there exists $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon) >0$, such that for all sufficiently large $n$, the sum of squares of the degrees of \emph{any} collection of $\delta n$ vertices is at most~$\varepsilon n$
nodes.label: lem:small-sq-nbd

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.2 (ii)
nodes.statement: Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Using Lemma~\ref{lem:small-sq-nbd}, let us choose $\delta_0= \delta_0(\varepsilon)>0$ such that $|U|\leq \delta_0n$ implies $\sum_{i\in U}d_i(d_i-1)<\varepsilon n$. Notice that if we blow up at most $\delta_0 n$ vertices, then the criticality parameter of the new graph changes by at most $\varepsilon n/\ell_n$, and thus for small $\varepsilon>0$, the blown up graph is also supercritical with high probability. Further, let $\mathcal{E}_k$ denote the event that the distance from bipartiteness of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$ is $k$. Thus, choosing $\delta<\delta_0$ small enough, Lemma~\ref{lem:prob-bipartite} yields \begin{equation} \prob{\mathrm{DistBip}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})})\leq \delta n}\leq \sum_{k=1}^{\delta n} {\ell_n/2 \choose k} \ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}(\mathcal{E}_k)\leq \sum_{k=1}^{\delta n} {\ell_n/2 \choose k}\ensuremath{\mathrm{e}}^{-C_0 n} \to 0. \end{equation} This completes the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:max-cut}~(ii).
nodes.statement_short: Union bound over sets of at most delta n edges: blowing up few vertices keeps the graph supercritical, and each such graph is bipartite with probability e^{-C_0 n}.

nodes.statement: The proof for the supercritical case (Theorem~\ref{thm:max-cut}~(iii)) uses the first moment method. For a set of vertices $A$, recall that $S(A)$ is the total number of half-edges associated with $A$, and $E(A,A^c)$ is the number of edges between $A$ and $A^c$.

nodes.name: Cross-edge distribution
nodes.statement: Partition the graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}$ in two parts $A$ and $A^c$, where we assume without loss of generality that $S=S(A)\leq \ell_n/2$. In this case, \begin{equation} \begin{split} \prob{E(A,A^c)=K}& = \frac{\binom{S }{K}K! (S-K-1)!! \binom{\ell_n-S }{ K}(\ell_n-S-K-1)!!}{(\ell_n-1)!!} \\ &= \exp\big(\ell_n f(x_n, y_n) (1+ o(1))\big) , \quad \text{where }\\ f(x, y) &= \ln\big(x^{x} (1-x)^{1-x}(1-x-y)^{-(1-x-y)/2}(x-y)^{-(x-y)/2}y^{-y}\big), \end{split} \end{equation} and $y_n = K/ \ell_n$, $x_n = S/ \ell_n$.

(S-K-1)!! \binom{\ell_n-S }{ K}(\ell_n-S-K-1)!!}{(\ell_n-1)!!} \\ &= \exp\big(\ell_n f(x_n, y_n) (1+ o(1))\big) , \quad \text{where }\\ f(x, y) &= \ln\big(x^{x} (1-x)^{1-x}(1-x-y)^{-(1-x-y)/2}(x-y)^{-(x-y)/2}y^{-y}\big), \end{split}
nodes.label: eq:upper_bound

nodes.name: Maximize at x=1/2
nodes.statement: We note that \begin{align} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} (x,y) = \ln \bigg(\frac{x}{1-x}\bigg) - \frac{1}{2} \ln \bigg(\frac{x-y}{1- x -y}\bigg). \nonumber \end{align} The fact that $x/(1-x) > (x-y)/(1-x-y)$ for any $0<y< x \leq 1/2$, implies that for any fixed $y$, $\{f(x,y): x \leq 1/2\}$ is maximized at $x=1/2$.
nodes.statement_short: The exponent is maximized at balanced half-edge split.

onumber\ &\hspace{1cm}\leq \sum_{S=1}^{\ell_n/2} \sum_{A: S(A) = S} \sum_{K= rac{\ell_n}{4}+ n c \sqrt{\mu}}^{S} \ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}\Big( E(A,A^c) = K \Big) 
onumber\ &\hspace{1cm}\leq 2^n \Big( rac{\ell_n}{2} \Big)^2 \max_{  rac{\ell_n}{4} + n c \sqrt{\mu} \leq K \leq  rac{\ell_n}{2}} \exp \Big[\ell_n f \Big( rac{1}{2},  rac{K}{\ell_n} \Big) (1+ o(1))\Big] . 
onumber \end{align}

nodes.name: Simplify exponent
nodes.statement: Writing $K/\ell_n = y$, notice that \begin{equation} \begin{split} &2^n\exp [\ell_n f(1/2,y)] \\ &=\exp\bigg[n\ln(2)+\ell_n\ln\bigg(\frac{1}{2}y^{-y}\Big(\frac{1}{2}-y\Big)^{-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}-y)}\Big(\frac{1}{2}-y\Big)^{-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}-y)}\bigg)+o(n)\bigg]\\ &= \exp\bigg[(1+o(1))\ell_n\ln\bigg(2^{1/\mu}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\Big(\frac{1}{2}-y\Big)^{-\frac{1}{2}+y}y^{-y}\Big)\bigg)\bigg], \end{split} \end{equation} since $\ell_n/n\to\mu$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite 2^n exp(l_n f(1/2,y)) as one exponent in l_n.

nodes.name: Exponent simplification at x=1/2
nodes.statement: \begin{split} &2^n\exp [\ell_n f(1/2,y)] \\ &=\exp\bigg[n\ln(2)+\ell_n\ln\bigg(\frac{1}{2}y^{-y}\Big(\frac{1}{2}-y\Big)^{-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}-y)}\Big(\frac{1}{2}-y\Big)^{-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}-y)}\bigg)+o(n)\bigg]\\ &= \exp\bigg[(1+o(1))\ell_n\ln\bigg(2^{1/\mu}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\Big(\frac{1}{2}-y\Big)^{-\frac{1}{2}+y}y^{-y}\Big)\bigg)\bigg], \end{split}

nodes.name: Combined bound
nodes.statement: Therefore, we obtain \begin{equation*} \begin{split} &\ensuremath{\mathbbm{P}}\Big({\sf{MaxCut}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})}) \geq \frac{\ell_n}{4} + n c \sqrt{\mu}\Big)\\ &\hspace{1cm}\leq \kappa n^2\max_{ \frac{1}{4} + \frac{c}{\sqrt{\mu}} \leq y \leq \frac{1}{2}} \exp\bigg[\ell_n\ln\Big(2^{\frac{1}{\mu}-1}\Big(\frac{1}{2}-y\Big)^{-\frac{1}{2}+y}y^{-y}\Big)\bigg], \end{split} \end{equation*}for some constant $\kappa>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the Max-Cut tail by a maximum over y.

nodes.name: Monotonicity in y
nodes.statement: Now observe that $\big(\frac{1}{2}-y\big)^{-\frac{1}{2}+y}y^{-y}$ is non-increasing in the interval $\big(1/4,1/2]$, and therefore the above maximum is attained at $y= \frac{1}{4} + \frac{c}{\sqrt{\mu}}$.
nodes.statement_short: The maximum is at the left endpoint y = 1/4 + c/sqrt(mu).

nodes.name: Define c*(mu) and conclude
nodes.statement: Define $$f(c,\mu):=\Big(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{c}{\sqrt{\mu}}\Big)^{-\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{c}{\sqrt{\mu}}\right)}\Big(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{c}{\sqrt{\mu}}\Big)^{-\left(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{c}{\sqrt{\mu}}\right)}-2^{-\frac{1}{\mu}+1} $$ and \begin{equation} c^\star(\mu)=\inf_{c>0}\Big\{c: f(c,\mu)<0 \Big\}. \end{equation} Thus, we can conclude that for any $c>c^\star(\mu)$, $$\prob{\frac{1}{n}{\sf{MaxCut}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{CM}_n(\boldsymbol{d})})>\frac{\mu}{4}+c\sqrt{\mu}}\to 0,\quad \text{as}\quad n\to\infty.$$
nodes.statement_short: Define f(c,mu) and c*(mu); for c>c*(mu) the bound vanishes.

nodes.name: Definition of c*(mu)
nodes.statement: c^\star(\mu)=\inf_{c>0}\Big\{c: f(c,\mu)<0 \Big\}.
nodes.label: eq:cstarmu

nodes.name: c*(mu) < sqrt(mu)/4
nodes.statement: Note that $f(0,\mu) = 2$, $\lim_{c\to (\sqrt{\mu}/4)^-}f(c,\mu) = \sqrt{2}$, and $f(\cdot,\mu)$ in strictly decreasing. Therefore, $c^\star(\mu)<\sqrt{\mu}/4$ for any $\mu>2$.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity and endpoint values of f(.,mu) bound c*(mu).

nodes.name: Large-mu asymptotics
nodes.statement: To see that $c^\star(\mu)\nearrow \sqrt{\ln(2)}/2$ as $\mu\nearrow\infty$, it can be checked using Taylor expansion with respect to $c$ around 0 that $f(c,\mu) \approx 2(1-2^{-1/\mu})-8c^2/\mu$. Also, for large $\mu$, $1-2^{-1/\mu}\approx \ln(2)/\mu$. Thus for large $\mu$, the value of $c^\star(\mu)$ is given by $\sqrt{\ln(2)}/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Taylor expansion shows c*(mu) tends to sqrt(ln 2)/2.
